person/chico-mendes.title: Chico Mendes
person/chico-mendes.summary: Chico Mendes (Francisco Alves Mendes Filho, 1944 to 1988) was a Brazilian rubber tapper, union leader and environmental activist in the state of Acre. He organized rubber tappers to defend the forest against clearing for cattle ranching and was murdered in December 1988.
facts: Chico Mendes was born on 15 December 1944 near Xapuri, Acre, into a family of rubber tappers (seringueiros).
He helped found the rural workers' union in Xapuri in 1977 and was among the founders of the Workers' Party in Acre in 1980.
He organized empates, non-violent standoffs in which tappers and their families stood in front of crews clearing forest.
In 1985 he helped found the National Council of Rubber Tappers, which promoted protected "extractive reserves" where residents could harvest forest products.
In 1987 he lobbied the Inter-American Development Bank in the United States over highway funding in the Amazon, and received a United Nations Environment Programme Global 500 award.
He was shot dead at his home in Xapuri on 22 December 1988. The rancher Darly Alves da Silva and his son Darci were convicted of the murder in 1990.
Extractive reserves became a legal category in Brazil in 1990.
person/chico-mendes.context: Chico Mendes worked in the Amazon Basin and South American Lowlands during the Information Age, amid the forest clearing of the Great Acceleration. The forest he defended has a long human history; see Amazonian Urbanism and Dark Earths. See Earth Systems and Life, Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
person/chico-mendes.observer: The Observer notes that Mendes joined a labor tactic, standing bodies in front of chainsaws, to an ecological argument, and that success came in the form of law only after his death. Ranchers described the forest as open land while tappers described it as a home and an income, so each side's claim-line rested on a different account of the same trees. A specialist could argue that extractive reserves have had mixed economic results for residents, which would weaken the claim that his approach protected both forest and livelihoods.
questions: How well have extractive reserves protected forest and livelihoods since 1990?

person/christopher-dresser.title: Christopher Dresser
person/christopher-dresser.summary: Christopher Dresser (1834 to 1904) was a botanist turned designer, now regarded as one of the first modern industrial designers. He worked as an independent consultant for dozens of manufacturers and produced geometric silverware and ceramics that anticipated 20th-century modernism.
facts: Dresser was born in Glasgow in 1834 and trained at the Government School of Design in London. He lectured on botany and in 1859 received a doctorate from the University of Jena for research into plant structure.

He moved into design from about 1858, with ceramic work for firms from the 1860s onwards (sources differ on the start), and published The Art of Decorative Design (1862) and Principles of Decorative Design (1873), arguing that ornament should follow the structural logic of natural forms rather than copy their surface.
In 1876 and 1877 he travelled to Japan, one of the first Western designers to do so, partly on commission from Tiffany & Co. to report on Japanese art and manufacturing.
He designed for Minton, Wedgwood, Coalbrookdale, Hukin & Heath and James Dixon & Sons, and was Art Superintendent of the Linthorpe Art Pottery. He died in 1904.

He reduced plants and shells to underlying geometry and embraced industrial methods, electroplating and moulded earthenware, that many reformers rejected. Key works include an electroplated teapot (1879), a toast rack (about 1880) and the Linthorpe "sea urchin" vase.

He was long overshadowed by William Morris and the craft wing of the Aesthetic Movement and has been substantially rediscovered since the late 20th century. His insistence that a mass-made object could be both functional and beautiful anticipated principles usually credited to the Bauhaus.
person/christopher-dresser.context: Dresser worked in Europe in the Industrial Age, designing for the machine at the height of the Industrial Revolution, in contrast to William Morris. See Art and Ritual and Technology.
person/christopher-dresser.observer: The Observer notes a botanist who built ornament from the structure of plants rather than their surface, and who accepted the machine that many contemporaries rejected. That his work was long overshadowed by the craft wing of his own movement shows a later story-glue about design, the handmade as honest, deciding which designers are remembered. His recent rediscovery as an ancestor of modernism is the reverse move, choosing a lineage backward. Both are readings of a body of objects that largely speak for themselves.
questions: How much of the work sold under his name was designed by him rather than by manufacturers' staff?

person/christopher-wren.title: Christopher Wren
person/christopher-wren.summary: Christopher Wren (1632 to 1723) was an English mathematician and astronomer, a founder of the Royal Society, who became an architect after the Great Fire of London in 1666. He designed more than fifty City churches and a new St Paul's Cathedral, topped out in 1708 and declared complete by Parliament in 1711.
facts: Wren was born in East Knoyle, Wiltshire, the son of a clergyman. He was appointed professor of astronomy at Gresham College at 25, then Savilian Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, and was a founding member of the Royal Society in 1662.
His architectural career began with the Sheldonian Theatre in Oxford. The Great Fire of September 1666 destroyed old St Paul's and most of the City.

He was appointed Surveyor of the King's Works in 1669 and spent the rest of his working life on the City's parish churches and on St Paul's. He died in 1723, aged 90, and is buried in the cathedral crypt.
He combined the classical vocabulary of Inigo Jones and Palladio with French and Italian Baroque elements he studied on a research trip to Paris, the only time he travelled outside England.
The dome of St Paul's is three independent shells nested inside one another, so that exterior profile, interior ceiling and structural core could each be optimised separately.
Key works include the Royal Observatory, Greenwich (1675 to 1676), the Royal Hospital Chelsea (1682 to 1692) and the Monument to the Great Fire (1671 to 1677).

Many City churches were later damaged or demolished, by Victorian redevelopment and by German bombing, but a substantial number still stand. Photographs of the dome above the smoke of the Blitz in 1940 circulated worldwide.
person/christopher-wren.context: Wren worked in Europe during the Early Modern Period and the Scientific Revolution, and drew on Andrea Palladio's classical vocabulary. See Art and Ritual, Science and Technology.
person/christopher-wren.observer: The Observer notes that a fire which destroyed a city also gave a mathematician the chance to become its chief builder, so that catastrophe became the hinge of a career and a skyline. The triple-shell dome is pattern-taming applied to stone. St Paul's later became a story-glue for national endurance through the photographs of 1940, a meaning laid on the building by later events rather than one Wren intended.
questions: Which of the City churches he designed survive in their original form?

person/cixi.title: Cixi
person/cixi.summary: The Empress Dowager Cixi (1835 to 1908) was the dominant political figure of late Qing China, ruling as regent for most of the period from 1861 to 1908.
facts: She became regent in 1861 for her young son, the Tongzhi Emperor, and later for the Guangxu Emperor.
Her period includes the Self-Strengthening Movement, an effort to modernize China's defenses and industry.
She supported the Boxers in 1900, and after their defeat she pursued the 'New Policies' reforms.
Historians debate her legacy; older accounts portray her as a reactionary, and recent work stresses her political skill and the limits she faced.
person/cixi.context: Cixi ruled the Qing Dynasty through the Opium Wars aftermath and the Boxer Rebellion. Compare Wu Zetian.
person/cixi.observer: The Observer notes that, as with earlier women rulers, the record on Cixi was written largely by her opponents. See Who Writes the Record.

person/claude-monet.title: Claude Monet
person/claude-monet.summary: Claude Monet (14 November 1840 to 5 December 1926) was a French painter, the leader and purest practitioner of Impressionism. His Impression, Sunrise gave the movement its name, and he spent his life painting the changing effects of light.
facts: Monet was born in Paris and grew up in Le Havre, where as a teenager he sold caricatures. Eugène Boudin persuaded him to paint outdoors. In Paris he met Camille Pissarro and befriended Renoir, Sisley and Bazille.
The 1860s and 1870s were years of poverty. During the Franco-Prussian War he took refuge in London, where he saw Turner's paintings and met the dealer Paul Durand-Ruel.
In 1874 he and his friends held an exhibition independent of the official Salon. Critics mocked them, and the name "Impressionist" stuck.
In 1883 his family settled at Giverny in Normandy, where he created a flower garden and a water garden with a Japanese bridge, which became his main subject.

He painted the same subject repeatedly in changing conditions: haystacks, poplars and Rouen Cathedral. Key works include Impression, Sunrise (1872), Stacks of Wheat (1890 to 1891) and the Water Lilies.
In his last decade he fought cataracts and worked on the giant Grandes Décorations, which he gave to the French state as a monument to peace after the First World War. He died at Giverny.
The Abstract Expressionists rediscovered his late water lilies in the 1950s. His house and gardens opened to the public in 1980, and in 2019 one of his Haystacks sold for $110.7 million.
person/claude-monet.context: Monet worked in Europe in the Industrial Age, learned from J. M. W. Turner and from Japanese prints by Katsushika Hokusai and Utagawa Hiroshige, and gave his last great work to France after World War I. See Art and Ritual.
person/claude-monet.observer: The Observer notes a painter whose subject was the act of seeing, and whose method, the same motif in changing light, shows that one scene is many scenes. A movement was named by critics who meant to mock it, and the name became a badge, so insult and category overlapped. His paintings later became commodities of very high price, $110.7 million for a Haystacks in 2019, a status-signal the critics of 1874 could not have predicted.
questions: How did his cataracts change the colour of his late paintings?

person/cleopatra-vii.title: Cleopatra VII
person/cleopatra-vii.summary: Cleopatra VII was the last active ruler of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, who allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony and died in 30 BCE after their defeat by Octavian.
facts: She belonged to the Ptolemaic dynasty, founded by a Macedonian general of Alexander the Great.
Ancient sources say she spoke several languages and, unlike most of her Ptolemaic predecessors, learned Egyptian.
She had a son with Julius Caesar and children with Mark Antony.
Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium in 31 BCE.
After her death in 30 BCE, Egypt became a Roman province.
person/cleopatra-vii.context: Cleopatra was a Greek-speaking ruler of the land of the Ancient Egyptians, descended from the generals of Alexander the Great. Her defeat by Augustus ended the last Hellenistic kingdom. Cleopatra VII sits in the Classical Antiquity and the region Nile Valley, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/cleopatra-vii.observer: The Observer notes that most of what is known about her comes from Roman authors who had reasons to portray her as a threat. The record was written by her enemies.
questions: How much of the traditional portrait comes from Roman propaganda?

person/confucius.title: Confucius
person/confucius.summary: Confucius (Kong Fuzi, 551 to 479 BCE) was a Chinese teacher and thinker whose ideas about ethics, family, and government shaped East Asian societies for over two thousand years.
facts: His sayings were collected by disciples in the Analects.
Central ideas include ren (humaneness), li (ritual propriety), and filial piety.
He was not widely influential during his lifetime; his ideas rose to prominence under the Han dynasty.
Confucian learning later became the basis of the imperial civil service examinations.
person/confucius.context: Confucius is one of the figures linked with the Axial Age. See Han Dynasty and East Asia.
person/confucius.observer: The Observer notes that a teacher without political power supplied the ethical framework of a large state. The kin-lattice, projected outward, became a model for government.
questions: How much of the Analects reflects Confucius himself?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Lived 551-479 BCE; Analects; ren, li and filial piety; not politically successful in life; Confucianism became state ideology under Emperor Wu of Han; examinations later centered on Confucian texts [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy on Confucius]

person/cyrus-the-great.title: Cyrus the Great
person/cyrus-the-great.summary: Cyrus the Great founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BCE by conquering the Medes, Lydia, and Babylon.
facts: His birth date is uncertain, with scholars giving about 600 to 576 BCE.
He defeated the Median king Astyages around 550 BCE and the Lydian king Croesus around 547 BCE.
He took Babylon in 539 BCE.
The Cyrus Cylinder, a Babylonian clay cylinder found in 1879, records his account of the conquest and his restoration of gods and deported peoples.
He died in 530 BCE campaigning on the eastern frontier and was buried at Pasargadae.
person/cyrus-the-great.context: Cyrus created the largest empire the world had yet seen, described in Achaemenid Persians. He is treated with respect in the Hebrew Bible and by Greek writers, including in the accounts of the Ancient Greeks. Cyrus the Great sits in the Iron Age and the region Iranian Plateau, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
person/cyrus-the-great.observer: The Observer notes that Cyrus is remembered as an unusually tolerant conqueror, mainly through his own inscription and the writings of those he benefited. The reading would change if evidence showed the tolerance was largely a later projection.
questions: How far does the Cyrus Cylinder reflect a real policy rather than propaganda?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Birth date uncertain; Astyages captured in 550 BCE; Babylon taken in 539 BCE; died 530 BCE; tomb at Pasargadae [World History Encyclopedia on Cyrus the Great]

person/darius-i.title: Darius I
person/darius-i.summary: Darius I (about 550 to 486 BCE) was king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire from 522 BCE. He organized its provinces, began the building of Persepolis, and recorded his rise to power in the Behistun Inscription.
facts: Darius I was born about 550 BCE and became king in 522 BCE after the death of Cambyses II. He put down revolts across the empire in his first years.

The Behistun Inscription, carved on a cliff in western Iran, tells the story of his rise in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Scholars debate whether its account of a usurper, Gaumata, is accurate, and Aramaic copies of the text have been found in Egypt.
He divided the empire into provinces (satrapies) under governors and issued a standard gold coin, the daric.
He is credited with the Royal Road from Sardis to Susa and began the terrace at Persepolis about 518 BCE, though sources differ and the earliest surviving remains there date to about 515 BCE.
His inscriptions honor the god Ahura Mazda.
After the Ionian Greek cities revolted in 499 BCE, he sent forces against Athens, and the Athenians defeated them at Marathon in 490 BCE.
Darius died in 486 BCE and was succeeded by Xerxes I.
person/darius-i.context: Darius ruled the Achaemenid Persians, founded by Cyrus the Great, from the Iranian Plateau during the Iron Age; see Persepolis. His wars involved the Ancient Greeks. See War and Conflict, Trade and Economy and Language and Writing.
person/darius-i.observer: The Observer notes that Darius told the story of his rise in stone, in three languages, on a cliff few could read, and sent copies across the empire. A multilingual empire needs a story-glue that works in several sound-codes, and a winner's account of a contested succession is a claim as much as a record. The reading would weaken if the usurper story proved accurate, since the inscription would then be closer to plain reporting.
questions: Was Gaumata a real usurper or an invention of Darius's court?

person/dido.title: Dido
person/dido.summary: Dido, also called Elissa, is the legendary founder-queen of Carthage, traditionally said to have led Phoenician settlers from Tyre to found the city on the North African coast around 814 BCE; her birth and death dates are not historically fixed.
facts: The earliest known account of her founding of Carthage comes from the Greek historian Timaeus of Tauromenium, writing in the 4th to 3rd century BCE, centuries after the traditional founding date.

Tradition holds she fled Tyre after her brother, King Pygmalion, murdered her husband to seize his wealth, and that she later took her own life rather than marry a local Libyan king, Iarbas, who threatened war.

No Phoenician inscription or contemporary record names a founder called Dido or Elissa; archaeological evidence of Phoenician settlement at the site of Carthage has so far been found only from the last quarter of the 8th century BCE, about a century or more after the traditional founding date, though it may still fit a folk memory of an organized colonizing expedition.

Her best-known appearance, as the doomed lover of the Trojan hero Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, is a literary invention: the Trojan War's traditional date is centuries before Carthage's traditional founding, so the two could not have met.
person/dido.context: Dido is remembered as the founder of Carthage, a Phoenicians colony in the Mediterranean Basin, placed in the Iron Age by tradition. See Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
person/dido.observer: The Observer notes that Dido's story likely preserves a genuine memory of Tyrian colonizing voyages, reshaped over centuries into the tale of one heroic founder, the way founding narratives often compress a longer, messier process into a single named person. Virgil's later romance with Aeneas shows how a founding legend keeps being rewritten to serve whichever storyteller's purposes come next.
questions: Does the Dido legend preserve any specific historical event, or is it entirely a later literary construction built around a folk memory of colonization?

person/diego-velazquez.title: Diego Velázquez
person/diego-velazquez.summary: Diego Velázquez (1599 to 1660) was the leading painter of Spain's Golden Age and court painter to King Philip IV for 37 years. His loose, luminous brushwork and unflattering portraits of kings, courtiers and jesters made him a "painter's painter".
facts: Velázquez was baptised in Seville on 6 June 1599. At about 11 he entered the workshop of Francisco Pacheco, and in 1618 he married Pacheco's daughter Juana. His early Seville work shows the influence of Caravaggio.
In 1623 a portrait of the young Philip IV won him the post of court painter, and he moved to Madrid. He rose through court offices to become chamberlain of the palace.

Peter Paul Rubens, on a diplomatic mission to Madrid in 1628, encouraged him to visit Italy. His first Italian trip (1629 to 1631) transformed his colour and handling. A second (1649 to 1651) produced his portrait of Pope Innocent X.
He painted Las Meninas in 1656 and in 1659 was admitted to the noble Order of Santiago, a rare honour for a painter. He died on 6 August 1660.
He painted alla prima, often without drawing, and altered compositions on the canvas; X-rays reveal many changes of mind. His palette was restrained, built on greys, blacks and earth tones.
His work stayed largely in Spanish royal palaces until the Prado opened in 1819. Manet travelled to Madrid in 1865 and called him "the painter of painters".
Picasso painted a series of 58 works on Las Meninas and related figures (1957), 44 of them variations on the whole painting, and Francis Bacon's screaming popes are based on his Innocent X.
person/diego-velazquez.context: Velázquez served the Spanish court in Europe during the Early Modern Period and began under the influence of Caravaggio. See Art and Ritual.
person/diego-velazquez.observer: The Observer notes a painter who recorded a king's heavy jaw and a court dwarf's dignity with the same honesty inside an institution built to display power, so that the candour worked within the status-signal machinery rather than against it. His work was kept in palaces until 1819, which makes his influence largely a nineteenth-century event. The title "painter of painters" is a lineage told by painters about a painter, a kind of ancestor-weight chosen rather than inherited.
questions: What do the changes of mind revealed by X-rays show about how he worked?

person/edvard-munch.title: Edvard Munch
person/edvard-munch.summary: Edvard Munch (12 December 1863 to 23 January 1944) was a Norwegian painter and printmaker who turned illness, grief, love and fear into images of inner states. The Scream became an emblem of the modern psyche, and he is a founding figure of Expressionism.
facts: Munch was born in Løten, Norway, and grew up in Kristiania (now Oslo). His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five and his sister Sophie of the same disease when he was 13. Another sister was later hospitalised for mental illness.
In the 1890s he lived mostly in Berlin and Paris and developed the Frieze of Life cycle. His 1892 exhibition in Berlin was closed after a week amid scandal, which made him famous in Germany.

He suffered a breakdown in 1908 and was treated in Copenhagen. From 1916 he lived at his estate, Ekely, outside Oslo. In 1937 the Nazis labelled his work "degenerate" and removed it from German museums.
He simplified forms into flowing outlines and flat expressive colour, influenced by Van Gogh, Gauguin and Symbolism. His woodcuts and lithographs are as important as his paintings.
Key works include The Sick Child (1885 to 1886), The Scream (1893), Madonna (1894) and The Dance of Life (1899 to 1900).
He left about 1,100 paintings, 4,500 drawings and 18,000 prints to the city of Oslo. The Scream has been stolen twice, in 1994 and 2004, and recovered both times.
person/edvard-munch.context: Munch worked in Norway, Germany and France, in Europe in the Industrial Age, and drew on Vincent van Gogh. See Art and Ritual.
person/edvard-munch.observer: The Observer notes a painter who said he painted what he had seen rather than what he saw, so that memory, not the eye, was the source of the image. The family record of early death and illness is part of how his work is read, which risks turning every picture into biography. That the Nazi label "degenerate" was applied to an artist now central to the canon shows how a state can act as a critic with the power to remove works from view.
questions: How far should the family history of illness govern the reading of his pictures?

person/eleanor-of-aquitaine.title: Eleanor of Aquitaine
person/eleanor-of-aquitaine.summary: Eleanor of Aquitaine (about 1124 to 1204, with older sources giving 1122 for her birth) was successively queen of France and queen of England, and one of the wealthiest and most powerful women in 12th-century Europe as ruler of the Duchy of Aquitaine in her own right.
facts: She inherited the vast Duchy of Aquitaine in southwestern France in 1137 and married King Louis VII of France that same year; the marriage was annulled in 1152 after producing no sons.

Weeks after the annulment she married Henry of Anjou, who became King Henry II of England in 1154, bringing her extensive French territories into the combined "Angevin Empire" that spanned much of France and England.
She supported a rebellion by three of her sons against Henry II in 1173 to 1174; after its failure, Henry kept her in confinement for about fifteen to sixteen years until his death in 1189.
Freed by her son Richard I ("the Lionheart"), she acted as regent during his crusade and captivity, and later helped secure the throne for her youngest son, John, after Richard's death in 1199.
person/eleanor-of-aquitaine.context: Eleanor of Aquitaine ruled territory in Europe during the Medieval Period, and her marriages linked the crowns of France and England. See Kinship and Society and War and Conflict.
person/eleanor-of-aquitaine.observer: The Observer notes that Eleanor's own duchy, not either crown she wore by marriage, was the base of her lasting power: it was Aquitaine's wealth and loyalty that gave her leverage over two kings and let her outlast a long confinement to shape the succession in her old age.
questions: How much independent political judgment did Eleanor exercise in backing her sons' rebellion, versus acting on their initiative?

person/eleanor-roosevelt.title: Eleanor Roosevelt
person/eleanor-roosevelt.summary: Eleanor Roosevelt (1884 to 1962) was First Lady of the United States from 1933 to 1945 and afterward a diplomat who chaired the United Nations commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
facts: She was born on 11 October 1884 in New York City and married Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1905.

As First Lady she redefined the role, holding her own press conferences, writing a daily newspaper column, and speaking for civil rights and the poor, sometimes publicly differing with her husband's policies.
After his death in 1945, President Truman appointed her a delegate to the new United Nations in December 1945.
She chaired the UN Commission on Human Rights, which drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the General Assembly on 10 December 1948. She called this her greatest achievement.
She later chaired a presidential commission on the status of women under President Kennedy.
She died on 7 November 1962 in New York City.
person/eleanor-roosevelt.context: Eleanor Roosevelt worked in North America during the Information Age, through World War II and into the early Cold War, when the United Nations was founded. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/eleanor-roosevelt.observer: The Observer notes that a document meant to bind every state to common claim-lines around a person's treatment was drafted under the chairmanship of a woman with no formal power beyond her office, relying on public standing built as a president's wife. The declaration is story-glue with no enforcement behind it, only the weight of near-unanimous agreement. A specialist could argue that the Declaration's later adoption by states party to it commits them to little in practice, which would weaken a reading of 1948 as a settled achievement rather than a beginning.
questions: How much practical effect has the Declaration had on states that signed it?
How much of her influence came from her own record, and how much from the Roosevelt name?

person/emperor-meiji.title: Emperor Meiji
person/emperor-meiji.summary: Emperor Meiji (1852 to 1912) was the Emperor of Japan from 1867, in whose name the Meiji Restoration transformed Japan into a modern industrial state.
facts: He came to the throne in 1867 at the age of about fourteen.
The Charter Oath (1868) was issued in his name, promising reform.
His reign saw a new constitution (1889), industrialization, and Japan's rise as a regional power.
He died in 1912.
person/emperor-meiji.context: He was the symbol of the Meiji Restoration that ended the Tokugawa Shogunate.
person/emperor-meiji.observer: The Observer notes that a young figure, whose real powers were exercised by advisers, gave legitimacy to sweeping change. The symbol of continuity can license a revolution.
questions: How much personal influence did the Emperor have?

person/enheduanna.title: Enheduanna
person/enheduanna.summary: Enheduanna (flourishing around 2300 BCE; the span of about 2285 to 2250 BCE is only an estimate) was a high priestess of the moon god Nanna at the Sumerian city of Ur and a daughter of Sargon of Akkad. She is often called the earliest author known by name, though her dates and the attribution of her texts are debated.
facts: Enheduanna served as en-priestess of Nanna at Ur, appointed by her father Sargon of Akkad. Her dates depend on the chronology used.
A disc found at Ur in 1927 by Leonard Woolley's team shows a figure identified by inscription as Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon, in a ritual scene.
Sumerian poems are attributed to her, including 42 temple hymns and hymns to the goddess Inanna such as "The Exaltation of Inanna."

The surviving copies come from schools of the Old Babylonian period, about 1800 BCE, some five to six centuries after her lifetime, and scholars disagree about whether she wrote every attributed text.
In "The Exaltation of Inanna" the speaker describes being driven from office by a usurper, Lugal-ane, and restored; the historicity of this is debated.
person/enheduanna.context: Enheduanna wrote in the Sumerian language of the Sumerians while serving a ruler from the Akkadian-speaking north, in Mesopotamia during the Bronze Age. Her work belongs to the story of the Invention of Writing. See Religion and Belief, Language and Writing and Art and Ritual.
person/enheduanna.observer: The Observer notes that a conquering dynasty placed a royal daughter at the head of a conquered city's main cult, a way of joining a new claim-line to old sacred authority through the kin-lattice. The same priestess is the first author recorded by name, so mark-code served a political and a devotional purpose at once. Because the texts survive only in later copies, the reading would weaken if the attribution to her proved to be a later tradition.
questions: Which of the texts attributed to her can be tied to her own time?

person/ezana-of-aksum.title: Ezana of Aksum
person/ezana-of-aksum.summary: Ezana was king of Aksum, in present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea, from about 320 to about 360 CE, though sources differ on the exact dates. He is known for adopting Christianity and for a campaign in the Nile valley, and his inscriptions and coins record both.
facts: Ezana came to the throne as a child and ruled the Kingdom of Aksum from about 320 until about 360. Dates for his life and reign are approximate, and sources differ.
His early inscriptions and coins show older Aksumite religion, including a crescent and disc on his coins.

Frumentius, a Christian from Tyre (described as Phoenician, and in some accounts Syrian) who rose in the Aksumite court, is reported to have been consecrated Aksum's first bishop by Athanasius of Alexandria, traditionally in 328, though other accounts say between 340 and 346.

Ezana converted to Christianity in the 4th century, though the exact date is uncertain. His later inscriptions invoke a "Lord of Heaven," and his coins replace the crescent and disc with the cross, which is often described as among the earliest coins to do so.
His inscriptions are in Ge'ez, Sabaean and Greek.
About 350 an Aksumite force campaigned in the Nile valley against Kush and neighboring peoples. The campaign is often linked to the end of Kush's power, though historians debate the causes.
person/ezana-of-aksum.context: Ezana ruled the Kingdom of Aksum and campaigned against the Kingdom of Kush in Sub-Saharan Africa during Classical Antiquity. See Religion and Belief, War and Conflict and Language and Writing.
person/ezana-of-aksum.observer: The Observer notes that a king's change of religion is visible in stone and coin: the same ruler's inscriptions change gods and his coinage changes symbols. A state's meaning-engine was switched from above and announced as a status-signal to the traders who used the coins across the Red Sea world. The reading would weaken if evidence showed that most of his subjects kept older practices for a long time after his conversion.
questions: When did his conversion take place, and how quickly was it announced?

person/francisco-goya.title: Francisco Goya
person/francisco-goya.summary: Francisco Goya (30 March 1746 to 16 April 1828) was a Spanish court painter and printmaker, often called the last of the Old Masters and the first of the moderns. Illness, political repression and the Napoleonic invasion drove him from brilliant royal portraits toward satire, violence and the irrational.
facts: Goya was born in Fuendetodos in Aragon and grew up in Zaragoza. In 1773 he married Josefa Bayeu, sister of the court painter Francisco Bayeu, who helped him win work designing tapestry cartoons in Madrid. By 1786 he was painter to the king, and in 1799 First Court Painter to Charles IV.
In 1792 to 1793 an illness left him permanently deaf. In 1799 he published Los Caprichos, satirical etchings mocking superstition and the clergy.

When Napoleon's armies invaded Spain in 1808 he witnessed atrocities on both sides and recorded them in The Disasters of War, prints published only 35 years after his death. He painted The Second and Third of May 1808 in 1814.

Disillusioned by the repressive rule of Ferdinand VII, he retreated to a house outside Madrid and covered its walls with the Black Paintings, including Saturn Devouring His Son (1819 to 1823). In 1824 he went into exile in Bordeaux, where he died.
His portraits, influenced by Velázquez, use loose brushwork and avoid flattery. He mastered aquatint for deep shadows and later applied paint with knives, rags and fingers.
Goya named Rembrandt as one of his three masters. Manet's Execution of Emperor Maximilian and Picasso's Guernica both descend from The Third of May.
The Prado holds the greatest collection of his work.
person/francisco-goya.context: Goya worked in Europe and lived through the Napoleonic Wars in the Industrial Age, learning from Diego Velázquez and Rembrandt van Rijn. See Art and Ritual and War and Conflict.
person/francisco-goya.observer: The Observer notes a court painter who recorded sanctioned harm from inside the society that practised it, and who kept the record private: The Disasters of War were withheld for 35 years. The same hand produced unflattering royal portraits and images of witches and monsters, which shows that the meaning-engine of the period, Church and crown, did not exhaust what one person could see. Later artists took his war images as a model, a case of ancestor-weight chosen by those who wanted a precedent for witnessing.
questions: Why did he withhold The Disasters of War, and what did he intend for the Black Paintings?

2026-09-27: At some time between late 1792 and early 1793 an undiagnosed illness left Goya deaf, and the aquatinted etchings begun afterwards were published in 1799 as the Caprichos. [Wikipedia on Francisco Goya]

person/frank-lloyd-wright.title: Frank Lloyd Wright
person/frank-lloyd-wright.summary: Frank Lloyd Wright (1867 to 1959) was the most influential American architect of the 20th century. Over seven decades he argued for "organic architecture", buildings designed from the inside out around their site, materials and users.
facts: Wright was born in Richland Center, Wisconsin, studied engineering briefly at the University of Wisconsin and moved to Chicago, where he worked under Louis Sullivan, whom he later called his "Lieber Meister".

He set up his own practice in Oak Park in the 1890s and developed the low, wide-eaved Prairie house style. His personal life was turbulent: an affair, the killing of seven people at his Wisconsin home Taliesin in 1914, and bankruptcy during the Depression.

In his late sixties he designed Fallingwater and the Johnson Wax headquarters (both 1936 to 1939), and finally the Guggenheim Museum (design and construction from 1943 to 1959). He died in 1959 aged 91.

He designed around open, flowing interior space, with art-glass bands and deep cantilevered overhangs, and used concrete, steel and glass without disguising them as historical stonework. He designed most of the furniture, textiles and stained glass in his buildings himself.
He designed more than a thousand structures, roughly half built. Fallingwater and several others are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Late in life he planned an unrealised city, Broadacre City, of low-density, car-based suburban living. He was also a major collector and dealer of Hiroshige's prints.
person/frank-lloyd-wright.context: Wright worked in North America in the Industrial Age and collected the prints of Utagawa Hiroshige. See Art and Ritual and Technology.
person/frank-lloyd-wright.observer: The Observer notes an architect whose principle was that a building grows from its site and its users rather than from a borrowed style, yet whose own name became a style. His open plan, now standard in American houses, shows a design idea spreading until it is no longer credited. Broadacre City, unbuilt, anticipated a pattern of car-based suburban living that later development followed, which suggests a vision can shape a society without being carried out by its author.
questions: How much of postwar suburban design can be traced to his ideas rather than to independent development?

person/frederick-barbarossa.title: Frederick Barbarossa
person/frederick-barbarossa.summary: Frederick I, called Barbarossa ("Redbeard"; about 1122 to 1190), was Holy Roman Emperor from 1155 until his death, and one of medieval Europe's most powerful rulers, spending much of his reign contesting control of northern Italy.
facts: Elected King of Germany in 1152, he was crowned Holy Roman Emperor by the pope in 1155, and repeatedly invaded Italy to assert imperial authority over its wealthy independent city-states.

The Lombard League, an alliance of northern Italian cities backed by the papacy, defeated his forces at the Battle of Legnano in 1176, forcing him to recognize significant city autonomy in the Peace of Constance of 1183.
He arranged the marriage of his son Henry to Constance of Sicily, a match that later brought the Kingdom of Sicily under his family's control.

He drowned in 1190 while crossing a river in Anatolia during the Third Crusade, before reaching the Holy Land; his death caused much of his army to disband or turn back rather than continue the campaign.
person/frederick-barbarossa.context: Frederick Barbarossa ruled the Holy Roman Empire in Europe during the Medieval Period, contesting authority with the papacy and Italian city-states. See War and Conflict, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
person/frederick-barbarossa.observer: The Observer notes that Barbarossa's defeat at Legnano, a rare and decisive loss for an emperor to city militias rather than a rival monarch, shows the limits of imperial authority once wealthy urban communities organized collectively. His accidental death crossing a river, not a battle, then ended a Crusade that a stronger start could not save from being cut short by chance.
questions: Would the Third Crusade's outcome for the German contingent have differed meaningfully had Barbarossa survived to reach the Holy Land?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Frederick was born in mid-December 1122, likely at Hagenau in the Duchy of Swabia, matching the note's date_start of 1122 [Wikipedia on Frederick Barbarossa]

2026-09-27: He was designated King of Germany by the princely electors at Frankfurt on 4 March 1152 and crowned Holy Roman Emperor by Pope Adrian IV at St Peter's Basilica on 18 June 1155 [Wikipedia on Frederick Barbarossa]

2026-09-27: He suffered a heavy defeat and was wounded at the Battle of Legnano near Milan on 29 May 1176 against the pro-papal Lombard League, and in the Peace of Constance of 1183 he conceded the towns' right to freely elect their magistrates [Wikipedia on Frederick Barbarossa]
2026-09-27: In 1186 he engineered the marriage of his son Henry to Constance of Sicily, heiress to the Kingdom of Sicily, over the objections of Pope Urban III [Wikipedia on Frederick Barbarossa]

2026-09-27: He drowned in the river near Seleucia on 10 June 1190 during the Third Crusade, after which several thousand German soldiers went home and only about 5,000, a third of the original force, reached Acre [Wikipedia on Frederick Barbarossa]

person/frida-kahlo.title: Frida Kahlo
person/frida-kahlo.summary: Frida Kahlo (1907 to 1954) was a Mexican painter, best known for small, vivid self-portraits made in Mexico City. She worked through years of pain after a bus accident in 1925 and became a global cultural icon after her death.
facts: Kahlo was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacán, now part of Mexico City. She often gave 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began, as her birth year.
A bus accident on 17 September 1925 broke her spine, pelvis and right leg and ended her plan to study medicine. She began painting during her recovery.
She married the muralist Diego Rivera in 1929, divorced him in 1939 and remarried him in 1940.
Estimates of her output run from fewer than 150 to about 200 paintings, most of them self-portraits, including The Two Fridas (1939) and The Broken Column (1944).
Her first solo show was at the Julien Levy Gallery in New York in 1938. In 1939 the Louvre bought her painting The Frame, the first work by a Mexican artist in its collection.
She died in Mexico City on 13 July 1954, officially of a pulmonary embolism. Her work was little known until art historians rediscovered it in the late 1970s.
person/frida-kahlo.context: Frida Kahlo worked in Mesoamerica during the Industrial Age, in the decades after the Mexican Revolution. See Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
person/frida-kahlo.observer: The Observer notes that a painter made her own body the subject of most of her work and moved her birth year to 1910, tying her life to a nation's revolution. Since the late 1970s her image has served as story-glue for movements that did not exist in her lifetime. A specialist could argue that this later fame flattens a private, ambivalent artist into an emblem, which would weaken any reading of the icon as what she intended.
questions: How much of her public persona did she shape herself, and how much was added after 1954?
What was the exact cause of her death?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Kahlo was born on 6 July 1907 in Coyoacan, and later began saying she was born on 7 July 1910, the year the Mexican Revolution began, to declare herself a daughter of the revolution [Wikipedia on Frida Kahlo]

2026-09-27: On 17 September 1925 a streetcar collided with the bus Kahlo was riding, leaving her with a broken spine, pelvis and right leg among other injuries, ending her plan to become a physician, and she began to paint while confined to bed [Wikipedia on Frida Kahlo]
2026-09-27: Kahlo married Diego Rivera on 21 August 1929, they divorced in 1939, and they remarried in a civil ceremony on 8 December 1940 [Wikipedia on Frida Kahlo]

2026-09-27: Kahlo died on 13 July 1954 aged 47, the official cause of death was pulmonary embolism although no autopsy was performed, and her work remained relatively unknown until the late 1970s [Wikipedia on Frida Kahlo]

person/fu-hao.title: Fu Hao
person/fu-hao.summary: Fu Hao (died about 1200 BCE) was a consort of the Shang king Wu Ding, named in oracle bone inscriptions as a military commander and a ritual leader. Her intact tomb, found in 1976, is among the richest of the Shang period. Her birth year is unknown.
facts: Fu Hao is named in oracle bone inscriptions as a wife of the Shang king Wu Ding, whose reign is dated about 1250 to 1192 BCE, though dates vary by chronology. She is thought to have died about 1200 BCE.
The inscriptions record her leading military campaigns against neighboring groups and directing ritual sacrifices.
Her tomb (M5) at Yinxu, the Shang capital site near Anyang in Henan, was found undisturbed in 1976 by a team led by Zheng Zhenxiang.
It held 468 bronze objects and 755 jade objects, as well as hundreds of bone objects and thousands of cowry shells.
Inscriptions on many bronzes name her, Fu Hao, or "Mother Xin," which is the basis for identifying the tomb with the woman of the oracle bones.
Sixteen people and six dogs were buried with her, interpreted as sacrifices.
person/fu-hao.context: Fu Hao lived under the Shang Dynasty in East Asia during the Bronze Age; her tomb shows the scale of Bronze Metallurgy in the Shang state. See War and Conflict, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
person/fu-hao.observer: The Observer notes that the earliest written evidence for a woman commanding armies comes from divination records made by her husband for other purposes, records that also ask about her illness and childbirth. Her burial, with a large store of bronze and jade and with human sacrifices, uses a grief-rite to display status. The reading of the tomb and the texts as one life would weaken if the oracle bone Fu Hao and the woman in tomb M5 were different persons.
questions: How large were the armies she led, and how reliable are the oracle bone figures?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Fu Hao died about 1200 BC and was one of the wives of the Shang king Wu Ding [Wikipedia on Fu Hao]
2026-09-27: Fu Hao served as a general in charge of several Shang military campaigns and as a high priestess who conducted rituals and oracle divination [Wikipedia on Fu Hao]

2026-09-27: Wu Ding's reign is dated c. 1250 to 1192 BC by the Xia-Shang-Zhou Chronology Project, while other chronologies (traditional, Bamboo Annals, radiocarbon) give different dates [Wikipedia on Wu Ding]

2026-09-27: Her tomb (M5) at Yinxu was unearthed intact in 1976 by a team led by the archaeologist Zheng Zhenxiang, and ritual bronzes inscribed with her name and the posthumous name Mu Xin (Mother Xin) identify it as hers [Wikipedia on Tomb of Fu Hao]

2026-09-27: The tomb held 468 bronze objects, 564 bone objects and about 6,900 cowry shells, with the skeletons of sixteen humans and six dogs interpreted as sacrificial burials [Wikipedia on Tomb of Fu Hao]

person/funmilayo-ransome-kuti.title: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti
person/funmilayo-ransome-kuti.summary: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900 to 1978) was a Nigerian teacher and campaigner who led the Abeokuta Women's Union in protests against a tax on women and against the local ruler, the Alake of Egbaland, in the 1940s.
facts: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti was born on 25 October 1900 in Abeokuta, in southwestern Nigeria. She studied there and in Cheshire, England, from 1919 to 1922.
In 1925 she married the Reverend Israel Oludotun Ransome-Kuti. Their children included the musician Fela Kuti and the physicians Beko and Olikoye Ransome-Kuti.
She founded the Abeokuta Ladies' Club in 1932. It became the Abeokuta Women's Union about 1946 and is reported to have had about 20,000 members.
In the late 1940s the union protested a tax on women and the rule of the Alake, Ademola II, who was forced to leave the throne for a time in 1949.
She helped found the Federation of Nigerian Women's Societies in 1953 and received the Lenin Peace Prize in 1970.

On 18 February 1977 soldiers stormed her son's compound in Lagos. Her family says she was thrown from an upper-floor window, and she died of her injuries on 13 April 1978. Official accounts blamed unknown soldiers.
person/funmilayo-ransome-kuti.context: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti worked in Sub-Saharan Africa in the years of Decolonization, during the Information Age. See Women's Suffrage Movements, Kinship and Society and Trade and Economy.
person/funmilayo-ransome-kuti.observer: The Observer notes that a claim-line between a colonial administration, a local king and a body of women, many of them market traders, was redrawn by organized refusal rather than by arms. The 1977 raid shows state force, once met with petitions, turned on her family. A specialist could argue that colonial officials' wish to avoid unrest mattered as much as the union's strength, which would weaken a reading that credits the organization alone.
questions: Who ordered and carried out the 1977 raid, and was anyone held responsible?
How much of the Alake's departure was caused by the union rather than by colonial officials' decisions?

person/galileo-galilei.title: Galileo Galilei
person/galileo-galilei.summary: Galileo Galilei (1564 to 1642) was an Italian scientist who used the telescope and experiments to support the Copernican view that the Earth orbits the Sun.
facts: In 1609 and 1610 he observed the Moon's mountains and four moons of Jupiter.
He studied falling bodies and motion using experiments.
In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried him and he was placed under house arrest for the rest of his life.
His 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' was published in 1632.
person/galileo-galilei.context: Galileo is a central figure of the Scientific Revolution and a predecessor of Isaac Newton.
person/galileo-galilei.observer: The Observer notes that his case shows two meaning-engines in contact: an institution that held authority over cosmology met a method that claimed authority through observation.
questions: How much did his trial turn on science versus politics?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Dialogue 1632; Inquisition verdict 22 June 1633; house arrest [Encyclopaedia Britannica; English Wikipedia]

person/genghis-khan.title: Genghis Khan
person/genghis-khan.summary: Genghis Khan (born Temujin, about 1162 to 1227) united the Mongol tribes in 1206 and founded the Mongol Empire.
facts: He built an army based on merit and loyalty rather than clan.
His campaigns overran Central Asia, northern China, and Persia.
He promoted a written script and a legal code (the Yassa) and encouraged religious tolerance.
He died in 1227; the location of his tomb is unknown.
person/genghis-khan.context: See Mongol Conquests and Mongol Empire. His empire brought the Central Asian Steppe to the center of Eurasian history.
person/genghis-khan.observer: The Observer notes that Genghis reorganized a kin-lattice into a merit-based institution, which is one of the roots of the empire's success and of its brutality.
questions: How reliable are the estimates of the deaths caused by his campaigns?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Proclaimed Great Khan 1206; died 1227; burial place unknown [Encyclopaedia Britannica; World History Encyclopedia]

person/georges-melies.title: Georges Méliès
person/georges-melies.summary: Georges Méliès (1861 to 1938) was a Paris stage magician who became a filmmaker and invented cinema's first special effects. Over roughly 500 films in under twenty years, including A Trip to the Moon (1902), he turned the new camera from a device for recording reality into a machine for staging the impossible.
facts: Méliès was born in Paris to a prosperous shoe-manufacturing family and wanted to study painting, but his father would not support him as an artist and he supervised machinery at the family factory. In about 1888 he bought the Théâtre Robert-Houdin, a famous conjuring theatre.

After attending the Lumière brothers' first public film screening in December 1895, he tried to buy a camera from them and was refused. He acquired one from a British inventor and built a studio at Montreuil with a glass-walled stage.

About 1896 he discovered, by accident when his camera jammed mid-shot, that stopping and restarting filming could make objects vanish or transform. This became the "stop trick" behind his trick films.
His techniques included stop-motion substitution, multiple exposure, dissolves, painted sets built to force perspective, and hand-tinted colour done frame by frame by a team of women colourists.
American piracy of his films, the rise of narrative studio filmmaking and the disruption of the First World War ruined his business. He was reduced to running a toy stall in a Paris train station.
He was rediscovered in his last decade, awarded the Légion d'honneur and, by some accounts, given a small pension. He died in Paris in 1938. Martin Scorsese's 2011 film Hugo dramatised his life.
Key works include The Vanishing Lady (1896), A Trip to the Moon (1902), The Kingdom of the Fairies (1903) and The Impossible Voyage (1904).
person/georges-melies.context: Méliès worked in France, in Europe in the Industrial Age, beside the Lumière Brothers, and his business collapsed in the aftermath of World War I. See Art and Ritual and Technology.
person/georges-melies.observer: The Observer notes a magician who saw in a recording device a stage: the same machine that recorded ordinary life in the Lumières' hands made the impossible in his. A camera jam is the standard account of the origin of the stop trick, the sort of founding accident a tool-lineage likes to remember, and it should be treated as an account rather than a proven event. That piracy and the market for narrative film ruined him shows an early case of the copy outrunning the maker.
questions: Did the camera jam actually happen as told, and when?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Georges Méliès was born on 8 December 1861 in Paris to a family whose father ran a boot factory on the Boulevard Saint-Martin, and he died in Paris on 21 January 1938 [Wikipedia on Georges Méliès]

2026-09-27: After attending a private Lumière demonstration on 27 December 1895 he offered 10,000 francs for one of their machines and was refused, then obtained an Animatograph projector from Robert W. Paul in London and modified it into a camera, and in September 1896 he built a glass-walled studio at Montreuil [Wikipedia on Georges Méliès]

2026-09-27: According to Méliès's own memoirs, the stop trick was discovered by accident when his camera jammed in the middle of a take, so the jam is his account rather than an independently documented event [Wikipedia on Georges Méliès]

2026-09-27: He directed over 500 films between 1896 and 1913, using techniques including multiple exposures, dissolves and hand-painted colour, and his works include The Vanishing Lady (1896), A Trip to the Moon (1902), The Kingdom of the Fairies (1903) and The Impossible Voyage (1904) [Wikipedia on Georges Méliès]

2026-09-27: Piracy by Edison and others, bankruptcy in 1913 after he broke his contract with Pathé and could not cover his debts, and the disruption of the First World War ended his filmmaking, after which he worked at a small candy and toy stand at the Gare Montparnasse; he received the Légion d'honneur in October 1931 and entered a retirement home in 1932 [Wikipedia on Georges Méliès]

person/gilgamesh.title: Gilgamesh
person/gilgamesh.summary: Gilgamesh was a king of the Sumerian city of Uruk, probably a real ruler of the Early Dynastic period sometime between about 2800 and 2500 BCE, who became the subject of the Epic of Gilgamesh, the earliest surviving major work of narrative literature.
facts: The Sumerian King List names him as the fifth king of Uruk's first dynasty and credits him with an implausible 126-year reign, typical of the list's treatment of early rulers.

Later inscriptions, notably the Tummal Inscription written under Ishbi-Erra long after the Early Dynastic period, credit a king of this name with building the great city walls of Uruk, a claim the Epic itself repeats as Gilgamesh's lasting achievement.

The Epic, assembled from older Sumerian poems into its best-known Akkadian version around the 12th century BCE, follows Gilgamesh's friendship with the wild man Enkidu, his quest for immortality after Enkidu's death, and his eventual acceptance of mortality.

No securely contemporary royal inscription from Gilgamesh's own lifetime has been found, though one inscription possibly from a contemporary official at Ur may name him; most of what historians infer about a real Gilgamesh comes from later king lists, dedicatory inscriptions naming him, and the literary tradition itself.
person/gilgamesh.context: Gilgamesh ruled Uruk among the Sumerians in Mesopotamia during the Bronze Age. See Religion and Belief, Kinship and Society and Art and Ritual.
person/gilgamesh.observer: The Observer notes that Gilgamesh sits at an unusual boundary: probably a real king, almost certainly not the demigod of the Epic, yet known to history mainly because later scribes turned him into a literary figure grappling with death rather than because his own deeds were separately recorded. The line between the ruler and the character is not fully recoverable.
questions: How much of the historical Gilgamesh's biography, beyond the city walls, can be separated from the literary tradition built around his name?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Scholars generally agree that Gilgamesh's lifetime lay between 2800 and 2500 BC, although precise dates cannot be given [Wikipedia on Gilgamesh]

2026-09-27: The Sumerian King List places Gilgamesh as the fifth ruler of the First Dynasty of Uruk with a reign of 126 years, and modern scholars caution that its early reign lengths are not reliable history [Wikipedia on Sumerian King List]

person/giotto.title: Giotto
person/giotto.summary: Giotto di Bondone (about 1267 to 1337) was a Florentine painter who gave medieval figures weight, emotion and space. Many call him the father of Western painting, and his frescoes in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua are his firmest work.
facts: Giotto was born about 1267, traditionally in the Mugello valley north of Florence, though his birthplace is disputed and some recent research points to Florence itself. Vasari's story of the shepherd boy discovered by Cimabue is legend, but he was almost certainly trained in Florentine workshops.

He was traditionally credited with the Legend of St Francis frescoes at Assisi in the late 1290s, but it is now generally accepted that four different hands are identifiable there and that they came from Rome, so his authorship is doubtful; his early career is still debated.
He painted the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua about 1303 to 1305 for the banker Enrico Scrovegni. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
He worked in Rome, in Santa Croce in Florence, and at the court of King Robert of Anjou in Naples from about 1328 to 1333.
In 1334 Florence named him master of works for the cathedral, and he designed its bell tower. He died in January 1337 and was buried with public honours.

He worked in buon fresco, painting into wet plaster one day's section at a time. His figures have volume and react to one another, and his spaces suggest depth more than 100 years before linear perspective was worked out.
In the chapel's Adoration of the Magi the star is painted as a blazing comet, perhaps inspired by Halley's Comet of 1301. The European Space Agency named its 1986 Halley probe Giotto.
Vasari opened his Lives of the Artists with Cimabue and Giotto. Masaccio and Michelangelo studied and copied Giotto's frescoes.
person/giotto.context: Giotto worked in Europe in the Medieval Period, before the Renaissance. See Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/giotto.observer: The Observer notes that the subject was fixed, the story of a meaning-engine repeated in every church, and that the change lay in how the story was made felt. Giotto's figures glance and grieve, so that sacred scenes read as human drama. The title "father of Western painting" comes largely from Vasari and later writers who needed a founder for a story of revival, which makes it partly a story-glue for art history rather than a plain finding. His early career remains debated, and the Assisi attribution is doubtful, since the St Francis cycle is now generally thought to be by Roman painters.
questions: How much, if any, of the Assisi Legend of St Francis cycle is by Giotto, given the now generally accepted view that it is by Roman painters?

2026-09-27: Around 1305 Giotto executed the interior frescoes of the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua, which Enrico degli Scrovegni commissioned as a family worship and burial space [Wikipedia on Giotto]
2026-09-27: In 1334 Giotto was appointed chief architect of Florence Cathedral and designed the bell tower (Giotto's Campanile), begun on 18 July 1334 [Wikipedia on Giotto]
2026-09-27: King Robert of Anjou called Giotto to Naples, where he remained with a group of pupils until 1333, and in 1332 named him first court painter with a yearly pension [Wikipedia on Giotto]

person/gitarja.title: Gitarja
person/gitarja.summary: Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi, known as Gitarja, was the third monarch of the Majapahit empire, reigning in Java from about 1328 to 1350; her birth is placed before 1309 and her death about 1372 to 1375, though both dates are uncertain.
facts: She became queen after the assassination of her half-brother Jayanegara in 1328 (the Nagarakretagama gives 1329 for her accession), ruling in the name of her mother, Gayatri Rajapatni, who had formally retired to a Buddhist convent.
Her chief minister, Gajah Mada, is credited with a famous oath to abstain from certain pleasures until he had brought the surrounding archipelago under Majapahit's authority.
Under her reign Majapahit forces conquered Bali in 1343, defeating the kingdoms of Pejeng and Bedahulu, a major step in the empire's expansion across the Indonesian archipelago.
She stepped down in 1350 after her mother's death and was succeeded by her son, Hayam Wuruk, under whom Majapahit reached its greatest territorial extent.
person/gitarja.context: Gitarja ruled Majapahit in Southeast Asia during the Medieval Period, and her minister's campaigns set up the empire's height under her son. See War and Conflict, Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
person/gitarja.observer: The Observer notes that Gitarja's reign is remembered mainly through the ambitions of her minister rather than any directly recorded decision of her own, a common pattern for royal women whose authority depended on men who did the fighting and the writing. Whether she directed Gajah Mada's campaigns or simply did not stop them cannot be recovered from the surviving sources.
questions: How much of Majapahit's expansion under Gajah Mada reflects Gitarja's own policy rather than his independent initiative?

person/gorgo.title: Gorgo
person/gorgo.summary: Gorgo (born about 518 BCE, last attested around 480 BCE) was queen of Sparta as the wife of King Leonidas I, remembered by the historian Herodotus as unusually sharp-witted and politically perceptive for a woman in his account of Greek affairs.
facts: She was the daughter of the Spartan king Cleomenes I and, according to Herodotus, advised him as a child not to trust a bribe offered by an Ionian envoy seeking Spartan military aid.

Herodotus credits her with detecting a warning about the Persian king Xerxes's invasion plans hidden on a wax-covered writing tablet sent by the exiled Spartan king Demaratus, when other Spartans could not work out its message.
She was the wife of Leonidas I, who died leading the defense of Thermopylae against the Persian invasion in 480 BCE, the same year in which she is last clearly attested in the sources.
Nearly everything known of her comes from Herodotus's Histories, written decades after her lifetime, and no independent Spartan record of her actions survives.
person/gorgo.context: Gorgo was queen of Sparta, part of the Ancient Greeks, in the Mediterranean Basin during Classical Antiquity. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/gorgo.observer: The Observer notes that Herodotus, writing for a Greek audience that saw Spartan women as unusually outspoken compared to other Greek women, may have shaped Gorgo's anecdotes to fit that reputation as much as to record specific events; the stories flatter both her personal intelligence and a wider Greek stereotype about Spartan women at the same time.
questions: How much of Gorgo's characterization in Herodotus reflects specific memory of her versus a general Greek stereotype about outspoken Spartan women?

person/gustav-klimt.title: Gustav Klimt
person/gustav-klimt.summary: Gustav Klimt (14 July 1862 to 6 February 1918) was an Austrian painter and the leader of the Vienna Secession. His golden, patterned paintings of women and love, above all The Kiss, are icons of turn-of-the-century Vienna.
facts: Klimt was born at Baumgarten near Vienna, the second of seven children of a gold engraver. He won a scholarship to the Vienna School of Arts and Crafts in 1876 and, with his brother Ernst and Franz Matsch, painted murals and ceilings for the Burgtheater and the Kunsthistorisches Museum.
In 1897 he became the first president of the Vienna Secession, a group breaking from the official academy with the motto "To every age its art, to art its freedom".

His ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna, showing Philosophy, Medicine and Jurisprudence, caused a scandal over nudity and pessimism. He withdrew from the commission, and the paintings were destroyed in a fire in 1945.

He never married, had a lifelong companionship with the designer Emilie Flöge and fathered several children with models. He supported younger artists such as Egon Schiele and Oskar Kokoschka. He died in Vienna after a stroke.

In his "golden period" (about 1899 to 1910) he applied real gold and silver leaf, drawing on Byzantine mosaics he saw in Ravenna in 1903, and on Japanese and Egyptian art. Key works include The Kiss (1907 to 1908) and the Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907).

Many of his works were owned by Jewish collectors and looted by the Nazis. The return of the Adele Bloch-Bauer portrait to Maria Altmann made headlines worldwide. Ronald Lauder bought it in 2006 for a reported $135 million.
In 2023 Lady with a Fan sold for £85.3 million, a record for a painting at auction in Europe.
person/gustav-klimt.context: Klimt worked in Vienna, in Europe in the Industrial Age, and died in the 1918 Influenza Pandemic. Works he painted were later looted in the Holocaust. See Art and Ritual.
person/gustav-klimt.observer: The Observer notes a movement whose motto framed art as a claim on institutions, and a painter who left a public commission when it drew scandal, so that a university, a meaning-engine of knowledge, refused images of its own faculties. The gold leaf and the auction records show the status-signal of the object at its extreme. Provenance adds a second biography: paintings taken from Jewish owners by the Nazis and later the subject of restitution cases carry sanctioned harm as part of their history.
questions: How many Klimt works taken from Jewish owners remain unrestituted?

person/hammurabi.title: Hammurabi
person/hammurabi.summary: Hammurabi was the king of Babylon from about 1792 to 1750 BCE, who united much of Mesopotamia and is known for a famous inscribed law code.
facts: The Code of Hammurabi, carved on a stone stele about 1754 BCE, lists 282 laws.
It sets penalties that vary by social class and includes the principle of proportionate punishment.
The stele was displayed publicly, making the law visible.
The original is in the Louvre in Paris.
person/hammurabi.context: Hammurabi ruled in Mesopotamia during the Bronze Age, inheriting the writing tradition begun by the Sumerians.
person/hammurabi.observer: The Observer sees a state converting custom into text. Putting law on stone changed what authority could claim: a rule that everyone can read, at least in principle, can bind the ruler as well as the ruled.
questions: How closely did courts follow the code?

person/harald-hardrada.title: Harald Hardrada
person/harald-hardrada.summary: Harald Hardrada (about 1015 to 1066) was King of Norway from 1046 to 1066, a warrior-king whose career took him from exile through mercenary service in Byzantium to the throne, and whose death at Stamford Bridge is often used to mark the end of the Viking Age.
facts: After his half-brother King Olaf II was killed in battle in 1030, the teenage Harald fled Norway and eventually served as a commander in the Byzantine Empire's elite Varangian Guard, campaigning in the Mediterranean and Middle East.
He returned to Scandinavia around 1045 with substantial wealth, and secured a share of the Norwegian throne in 1046, becoming sole king after his co-ruler's death in 1047.
He fought years of inconclusive war against Denmark over rival claims, finally making peace in 1064 (or 1065 according to Morkinskinna) without gaining the Danish throne he sought.

He invaded England in September 1066 to press a rival claim to its throne, but was defeated and killed at the Battle of Stamford Bridge by King Harold Godwinson, days before Godwinson had to march south to face William of Normandy's invasion at Hastings.
person/harald-hardrada.context: Harald Hardrada led the Norse as King of Norway, in Europe, during the Medieval Period. See War and Conflict and Trade and Economy.
person/harald-hardrada.observer: The Observer notes that Harald's failed invasion, remembered mainly as a footnote to the Norman Conquest, forced Harold Godwinson's army into an exhausting march across England that arguably weakened it before Hastings; a defeat at Stamford Bridge may have shaped the more famous battle that followed it more than its traditional label as a mere prelude suggests.
questions: How much did the English army's losses and exhaustion at Stamford Bridge actually affect its performance three weeks later at Hastings?

person/harriet-tubman.title: Harriet Tubman
person/harriet-tubman.summary: Harriet Tubman (about 1822 to 1913) was an American abolitionist who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and then guided others to freedom on the Underground Railroad. She later served the Union Army in the Civil War.
facts: Tubman was born Araminta Ross into slavery in Dorchester County, Maryland; her birth year is uncertain, with sources giving dates from 1815 to 1825 and about 1822 the most favoured.
As a teenager she suffered a severe head injury when an overseer threw a metal weight, and had seizures and headaches for the rest of her life.
She escaped to Pennsylvania in 1849 and afterward made about 13 trips back to Maryland, guiding roughly 70 people to freedom, according to her biographers.

During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a cook, nurse, scout and spy. In June 1863 she helped guide the Combahee River Raid in South Carolina, which freed more than 700 enslaved people, though some sources give more than 750.
After the war she lived in Auburn, New York, where she cared for her family and for elderly people, and she worked for women's suffrage.
She died in Auburn on 10 March 1913.
person/harriet-tubman.context: Tubman opposed slavery in the United States, part of the wider history of the Abolition of Slavery, and served in the American Civil War in North America during the Industrial Age. See also Women's Suffrage Movements, War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/harriet-tubman.observer: The Observer notes that a rescue network that depended on secrecy left little paper, so the record of Tubman's trips rests on her own recollections as told to others, since she could not write. Her escape became a repeated and organized risk carried out through families and congregations, a kin-lattice used as a channel for hidden information. The reading of the counts of trips and people as estimates would weaken if newly found records fixed them.
questions: How well do surviving records support the counts of her rescue trips?

person/hatshepsut.title: Hatshepsut
person/hatshepsut.summary: Hatshepsut was an Egyptian ruler of the 18th Dynasty who held the title of pharaoh, sharing the throne with Thutmose III, until her death in 1458 BCE. Her reign is traditionally dated 1479 to 1458 BCE, and she is one of the first women known to have held the office.
facts: She first acted as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, then took the title of pharaoh around the seventh year of his reign (about 1473 BCE), sharing his regnal count.
She sponsored a trading expedition to Punt, on the Red Sea coast of Africa.
Her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari is a major monument.
Many of her images were later removed or defaced, possibly after her death.
person/hatshepsut.context: Hatshepsut is a figure of the Ancient Egyptians in the Bronze Age. Her reign shows how kingship in the Nile Valley could accommodate a woman ruler.
person/hatshepsut.observer: The Observer notes how she was shown with the regalia and beard of a male king. The kingship, a role bound to cosmic order, mattered more than the sex of its holder, until later authorities erased her image.
questions: Why were her monuments defaced?

person/henry-ossawa-tanner.title: Henry Ossawa Tanner
person/henry-ossawa-tanner.summary: Henry Ossawa Tanner (21 June 1859 to 25 May 1937) was an American painter, the first African American artist to win international fame. Frustrated by racism at home, he settled in Paris in 1891 and built his career there, painting dignified genre scenes and luminous biblical subjects.
facts: Tanner was born in Pittsburgh, the eldest of nine children. His father, Benjamin Tucker Tanner, became a bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and his mother, Sarah, had escaped slavery via the Underground Railroad. At 13 he decided to become an artist.

In 1879 he enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and studied with Thomas Eakins. He was the only Black student and faced harassment. He left for Europe in 1891 and studied at the Académie Julian in Paris.
On a return visit in 1893 he painted The Banjo Lesson, and he painted The Thankful Poor in 1894, both genre scenes of Black American life that challenged racist stereotypes.

Back in France he turned to biblical subjects. The Resurrection of Lazarus won a medal at the 1897 Salon, and the French government bought it. His patron Rodman Wanamaker paid for trips to Egypt and Palestine.
He married the singer Jessie Olsson in 1899. He was made a Chevalier of the Légion d'honneur in 1923 and died in Paris.
He preferred a limited palette of deep blues and blue-greens with glowing gold highlights, built up in layers of glaze.

He advised younger painters such as William Edouard Scott and Hale Woodruff, and was a hero to the artists of the Harlem Renaissance. During the Clinton administration, reportedly in 1996, his Sand Dunes at Sunset, Atlantic City became the first painting by an African American artist in the White House collection.
person/henry-ossawa-tanner.context: Tanner worked mostly in France, in Europe, in the Industrial Age, as an American artist. See Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/henry-ossawa-tanner.observer: The Observer notes a painter who left a country whose art institutions harassed him and built a career in another, where the salon judged the paintings. His two bodies of work, genre scenes of Black life and biblical scenes using ordinary people as models, both aimed at truth over caricature, and both answered a stereotype without naming it. That the first painting by an African American artist entered the White House collection only under the Clinton administration shows how slowly an institution's memory catches up with a reputation.
questions: How did his French reception differ from what he would have faced in the United States?

person/hieronymus-bosch.title: Hieronymus Bosch
person/hieronymus-bosch.summary: Hieronymus Bosch (about 1450 to 1516) was a painter from 's-Hertogenbosch in the Duchy of Brabant who filled his panels with hybrid monsters and crowds of tiny figures acting out human sin and folly. Only about 25 paintings are firmly attributed to him.
facts: Bosch was born Jheronimus van Aken about 1450 in 's-Hertogenbosch. His grandfather, father and uncles were painters, and he later signed his works "Jheronimus Bosch" after the town.

Sometime between 1479 and 1481 he married Aleid Goyaerts van den Meervenne, of a wealthy family. In 1486 or 1487 he became a sworn member of the Illustrious Brotherhood of Our Blessed Lady, and he died in 1516.

He seems to have spent almost his whole life in and near 's-Hertogenbosch, and after marrying he and Aleid moved to nearby Oirschot, yet his fame spread. Philip the Handsome, Duke of Burgundy, commissioned a Last Judgment from him in 1504.

He painted in oil on oak panels, often as triptychs. Key works include The Garden of Earthly Delights (about 1495 to 1505), The Ship of Fools (about 1500 to 1510), The Temptation of St Anthony (about 1501) and the Haywain Triptych (about 1510 to 1516).
King Philip II of Spain acquired many Bosch paintings in the late 16th century, which is why the Prado in Madrid holds his greatest paintings.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder built on his crowded moral landscapes. After being partly forgotten, Bosch was claimed in the 20th century by Surrealists such as Salvador Dalí and Max Ernst.

In 2016, the 500th anniversary of his death, the Bosch Research and Conservation Project re-examined his works, and several attributions changed in both directions, with a Temptation of St Anthony credited to Bosch himself after being given to his workshop, and other works questioned as workshop pieces.
person/hieronymus-bosch.context: Bosch worked in Europe in the Medieval Period, at the time of the Renaissance. See Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/hieronymus-bosch.observer: The Observer notes a painter who gave visible form to the fears of a meaning-engine, hell, folly and temptation, in crowded panels meant to be read slowly and closely. The same images were later read by Surrealists as dreams, so what the pictures meant changed with the audience. With only about 25 firmly attributed works and reattributions as recent as 2016, the artist himself is still being redrawn, and any account of what he intended should be held loosely.
questions: Which works are by Bosch himself and which by his workshop?
What did the imagery mean to the people who first saw it?
