person/hilma-af-klint.title: Hilma af Klint
person/hilma-af-klint.summary: Hilma af Klint (26 October 1862 to 21 October 1944) was a Swedish painter who, from 1906, created hundreds of abstract paintings guided by her spiritual beliefs, several years before Kandinsky, Mondrian and Malevich. She kept them largely hidden, and they reached an international audience only from the 1980s.
facts: Af Klint was born at Karlberg Palace in Solna, near Stockholm. She studied at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Stockholm from 1882 to 1887 and made a living painting landscapes, portraits and botanical illustrations.

Her spiritual investigations, which sources date from 1879, developed around the time of the death of her younger sister Hermina in 1880 and drew her toward spiritualism and Theosophy. With four other women, who began as members of the Edelweiss Society, she made up "The Five", which held séances and experimented with automatic drawing, which the sources date to 1896.

In 1906, believing she had received a commission from a spiritual guide, she began the Paintings for the Temple, a cycle of nearly 200 works completed in 1915. She considered herself a medium through whom the works were created.

In 1908 she showed her work to Rudolf Steiner. His cool response contributed to a four-year break in the series. She later spent long periods at the Goetheanum, the Anthroposophical Society's headquarters, between 1921 and 1930, and filled more than 125 notebooks, with sources giving figures from 125 to more than 150.

She believed the world was not ready for the paintings and directed that they not be exhibited until 20 years after her death. She died after a traffic accident, leaving more than 1,200 paintings and drawings to her nephew.

Her abstract works combine geometric and organic forms with letters and symbols. In her colour code blue often stood for the female spirit, yellow for the male spirit and pink or red for physical and spiritual love. She drew on Theosophy, Christianity, botany and the new sciences of evolution and atomic physics.

She exhibited only a handful of times in her lifetime, mostly at spiritual conferences. Her work reached an international audience in the 1980s, including in the 1986 exhibition The Spiritual in Art at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. The Guggenheim's Paintings for the Future (2018 to 2019) drew more than 600,000 visitors, the most visited exhibition in its history.
person/hilma-af-klint.context: Af Klint worked in Sweden, in Europe in the Industrial Age. See Art and Ritual, Religion and Belief and Science.
person/hilma-af-klint.observer: The Observer notes work made for a temple of a meaning-engine rather than for a market, and withheld by its maker because she thought the world was not ready, so that art history was written for about eight decades without it. She framed authorship as mediumship, which sits awkwardly with the modern habit of crediting an individual inventor. The claim that she "invented abstraction" before Kandinsky depends on dating the works and defining abstraction, and the question of who was first is a story-glue of art history.
questions: How should the date and priority of her abstraction be weighed against those of Kandinsky, Mondrian and Malevich?

person/ho-chi-minh.title: Ho Chi Minh
person/ho-chi-minh.summary: Ho Chi Minh (1890 to 1969) was a Vietnamese revolutionary who led the movement against French rule, headed the provisional government in 1945, and became the first president of the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in 1946, an office he held until his death during the Vietnam War.
facts: He was born on 19 May 1890 in Nghệ An province, French-ruled Vietnam, as Nguyễn Sinh Cung, and later used many names, including Nguyễn Ái Quốc and, from about 1943, Hồ Chí Minh.
He left Vietnam in 1911 and lived in Britain, France, the Soviet Union and China. In early 1930, in Hong Kong, he chaired the merger of Vietnamese communist groups into one party.

He returned to Vietnam in 1941 to lead the Việt Minh independence front, and on 2 September 1945 in Hanoi read the declaration of independence, opening by quoting the American and French declarations of rights.
The First Indochina War ended with the Việt Minh victory at Điện Biên Phủ in 1954. Vietnam was partitioned at the 17th parallel, and the 1956 reunification elections were never held.
In the North's 1953 to 1956 land reform, many people were wrongly executed, with estimates from about a thousand to tens of thousands; he apologized in 1956 for serious errors.
He died in Hanoi on 2 September 1969. Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City after reunification in 1975.
person/ho-chi-minh.context: Ho Chi Minh worked in Southeast Asia during the Information Age, in the years of Decolonization and the Cold War. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/ho-chi-minh.observer: The Observer notes that a man who used dozens of names became the named symbol of a nation, and his declaration borrowed the mark-code of the powers he opposed. His name now marks the largest city of the country he did not live to see reunified. A specialist could argue that party and army leaders, more than one man, drove decisions in the 1960s, which would weaken a reading that centers his person.
questions: How many people were executed in the land reform, and what did he know of it?
How much did he direct the war after the early 1960s?

person/hojo-tokimune.title: Hojo Tokimune
person/hojo-tokimune.summary: Hojo Tokimune (1251 to 1284) was the eighth regent (shikken) of Japan's Kamakura shogunate, ruling as its de facto military leader during the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274 and 1281.
facts: He became regent in 1268 at about age sixteen by Western reckoning (eighteen by traditional counting), shortly after the Mongol court of Kublai Khan first demanded Japan's submission.
He refused all Mongol diplomatic demands and reportedly had several Mongol envoys executed, a decision that made war effectively certain.

Japanese defenders repelled the 1274 and 1281 Mongol invasion fleets; in 1281 a great typhoon and, in 1274, traditionally a storm or sudden reverse wind, later remembered as kamikaze ("divine wind"), destroyed large parts of the Mongol fleets after the defenders had already inflicted losses on the invading forces.
He was a patron of Zen Buddhism, inviting the Chinese monk Wuxue Zuyuan to Kamakura and founding the temple Engaku-ji, reportedly to honor the dead of both sides after the invasions.
person/hojo-tokimune.context: Hojo Tokimune governed Kamakura Japan in East Asia during the Medieval Period, defending against the Mongol Empire at the height of its westward and eastward expansion. See War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
person/hojo-tokimune.observer: The Observer notes that the "divine wind" traditionally said to have ended both invasions has often overshadowed the more mundane fact that Japanese defenders, organized under Tokimune's government, had already stalled both landings before the storms struck, while the coastal fortifications such as the Hakata Bay wall were built in 1276, after the first invasion. Crediting the weather alone understates the preparation his regency undertook.
questions: How much of the invasions' failure owed to the storms versus the defensive tactics, and for 1281 the walls, that Tokimune's government had built along Hakata Bay?

person/hypatia.title: Hypatia
person/hypatia.summary: Hypatia (about 350 to 415 CE) was a philosopher, mathematician, and astronomer in Alexandria, who taught many students and was murdered by a mob.
facts: She was the daughter of the mathematician Theon and taught Neoplatonist philosophy.
She is credited with commentaries on mathematical works; the details are uncertain.
In 415 she was killed by a Christian mob during a political dispute between the Roman governor Orestes and Bishop Cyril.
Later writers turned her into a symbol, so historical and legendary accounts are mixed.
person/hypatia.context: Hypatia worked in Roman Egypt, in the Nile Valley, at the end of Classical Antiquity. She continued the tradition of Aristotle and his successors.
person/hypatia.observer: The Observer notes that a scholar became a symbol after her death, used by later writers for their own purposes. Legends grow around individuals in ways that can obscure the historical person.
questions: What did Hypatia actually write?

person/ibn-battuta.title: Ibn Battuta
person/ibn-battuta.summary: Ibn Battuta (1304 to about 1369) was a Moroccan scholar and traveler whose account, the Rihla, describes journeys of about 117,000 kilometers (73,000 miles) across much of the Old World.
facts: He left Tangier in 1325 for a pilgrimage and kept traveling for about 30 years.
He visited Arabia, East Africa, Persia, India, Southeast Asia, and the Mali Empire (1352 to 1353).
His account was dictated to the scholar Ibn Juzayy.
Historians debate whether he actually visited all of the places he describes.
person/ibn-battuta.context: He traveled within the world of the Indian Ocean Trade Network, visiting Swahili Coast City-States and the Mali Empire.
person/ibn-battuta.observer: The Observer notes that a person could travel most of the known world, and be received as a scholar, because a shared religion and law provided a common frame. The Islamic world worked as one large, connected network.
questions: How reliable is the Rihla as a record of his journeys?

person/ibn-khaldun.title: Ibn Khaldun
person/ibn-khaldun.summary: Ibn Khaldun (1332 to 1406) was a North African historian whose 'Muqaddimah' (1377) proposed a general theory of how societies and states rise and fall.
facts: He was born in Tunis and served in several courts in North Africa and Andalusia.
He argued that group solidarity (asabiyyah) helps found dynasties, and that as rulers grow comfortable it weakens.
He wrote about economics, urban life, and the role of climate and environment.
He is sometimes called a founder of sociology and historiography.
person/ibn-khaldun.context: Ibn Khaldun wrote in the world of Ibn Battuta and recorded facts about the Mali Empire. His approach is close to the Observer's own.
person/ibn-khaldun.observer: The Observer notes that Ibn Khaldun was doing 'anthropology of the species' six centuries ago: looking for patterns in how groups rise and fall, rather than for the will of individuals. He is a precursor of the Observer's method.
questions: How well does his cycle of dynasties fit the historical record?

person/ibn-sina.title: Ibn Sina
person/ibn-sina.summary: Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980 to 1037) was a Persian physician and philosopher whose 'Canon of Medicine' became a standard medical text in the Islamic world and Europe for centuries.
facts: He was born near Bukhara in Central Asia.
The Canon of Medicine (completed about 1025) organized medical knowledge in a systematic way.
It was translated into Latin and used in European universities into the 17th century.
His philosophical 'Book of Healing' also influenced medieval Europe.
person/ibn-sina.context: Ibn Sina drew on the tradition of the Translation Movement and the House of Wisdom and the wider Abbasid Caliphate world.
person/ibn-sina.observer: The Observer notes that a single reference book could organize the medical practice of many societies. Standard texts are a form of story-glue for a profession.
questions: How much of the Canon was original versus a synthesis?

person/indira-gandhi.title: Indira Gandhi
person/indira-gandhi.summary: Indira Gandhi (1917 to 1984) was prime minister of India for most of 1966 to 1984. She led India through the 1971 war that created Bangladesh, imposed emergency rule from 1975 to 1977, and was assassinated by her own bodyguards after ordering an army raid on Sikhism's holiest shrine.
facts: She was born on 19 November 1917 in Allahabad, daughter of Jawaharlal Nehru, India's first prime minister, and became prime minister herself in 1966.
In 1971 India backed the independence of East Pakistan, which became Bangladesh, after a short war with Pakistan.
On 25 June 1975 she had a state of emergency declared, suspending civil liberties, censoring the press and jailing opponents, until elections in 1977 that she lost.
She returned to power in 1980. Government policy also pushed the Green Revolution's higher-yield crops during her years in office.
In June 1984 she ordered Operation Blue Star, a military assault on the Golden Temple in Amritsar to remove armed Sikh militants, which damaged the shrine and angered many Sikhs.
On 31 October 1984 two of her Sikh bodyguards assassinated her in New Delhi. Riots afterward killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi.
person/indira-gandhi.context: Indira Gandhi led India in South Asia during the Information Age, a state formed after the Partition of India. See War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
person/indira-gandhi.observer: The Observer notes that a leader who suspended the young republic's own rules in 1975 was, nine years later, killed for ordering force against a meaning-engine's holiest site, and that sanctioned harm against her spread outward into killing among ordinary Sikhs. A specialist could argue that Operation Blue Star addressed an armed occupation of the temple and was not aimed at Sikh belief itself, which would weaken a reading of the raid as simple religious attack.
questions: How far did the 1975 Emergency reflect a threat to her rule, and how far a choice to entrench it?
What did she foresee for the Sikh community after Operation Blue Star?

person/isaac-newton.title: Isaac Newton
person/isaac-newton.summary: Isaac Newton (1642 to 1727) was an English mathematician and physicist whose laws of motion and universal gravitation formed the basis of classical mechanics.
facts: His 'Principia' (1687) presents the laws of motion and the law of gravitation.
He developed calculus, independently of Leibniz, leading to a priority dispute.
He studied optics, showing that white light is composed of colors.
He also spent much time on alchemy and theology.
person/isaac-newton.context: Newton completed the work of the Scientific Revolution begun by Galileo Galilei. His physics framed science until the time of Albert Einstein.
person/isaac-newton.observer: The Observer notes that Newton showed the same rules govern falling apples and orbiting planets. It was a demonstration that the species could find laws that hold everywhere it looked.
questions: How should his interest in alchemy be understood alongside his physics?

person/j-m-w-turner.title: J. M. W. Turner
person/j-m-w-turner.summary: Joseph Mallord William Turner (April 1775 to 19 December 1851) was the greatest British landscape painter and a bold colourist. He began as a precise topographical watercolourist, and his late paintings dissolve ships, trains and cities into light, mist and weather.
facts: Turner was born in Covent Garden, London, the son of a barber and wigmaker. At 14 he entered the Royal Academy Schools and at 15 exhibited his first watercolour. He was elected a full Royal Academician in 1802, at 26 or 27 depending on the source.
He travelled tirelessly in Britain, the Alps, France, Germany and Italy, especially Venice, filling hundreds of sketchbooks.
He never married but had two daughters with Sarah Danby. John Ruskin championed him in Modern Painters (1843). He died in Chelsea and was buried in St Paul's Cathedral.
By the 1830s he painted natural forces themselves, storms, fire, sunlight and steam. He worked thin washes over white grounds, scraped and rubbed his canvases, and applied paint thickly with knives.
He painted steamships and railways alongside Venetian lagoons. Rain, Steam and Speed (1844) is one of the first great paintings of modern technology.

The Slave Ship (1840) was possibly inspired by the Zong massacre of 1781, when enslaved Africans were thrown overboard so owners could claim insurance. He showed it during the 1840 campaign to end slavery worldwide.

He left around 300 oil paintings and over 19,000 sketches, drawings and watercolours and some 200 sketchbooks to the nation, held mainly at Tate Britain. Monet and Pissarro studied his work in London in 1870 to 1871, and the Turner Prize has been awarded since 1984.
person/j-m-w-turner.context: Turner painted the Industrial Revolution and its Railways in Europe during the Industrial Age, and in The Slave Ship confronted the Atlantic Slave Trade. See Art and Ritual and Technology.
person/j-m-w-turner.observer: The Observer notes a painter who put a steam train and a slave ship into the same body of work, the two great tool-lineages of his century, one celebrated and one condemned, both moving people and goods across water and land. Critics who mocked his late style were reading a change in how the species pictures weather and speed. That he left his work to the nation and gave a prize its name shows a personal reputation converted into an institution, a story-glue for national art.
questions: How did his late style change how contemporaries saw landscape, given the criticism it drew?

person/jadwiga.title: Jadwiga
person/jadwiga.summary: Jadwiga (about 1373 to 1399) was crowned "King" of Poland in 1384 at about age ten, often described as the first woman to rule Poland in her own right, and her marriage to the Grand Duke of Lithuania began a dynastic union between the two states.
facts: She was crowned using the male title "rex" (king) rather than "regina" (queen) to underscore that she held full sovereign authority in her own right, not merely as a royal consort.

In 1386 she married Jogaila, the pagan Grand Duke of Lithuania, who converted to Christianity and was crowned co-ruler as Wladyslaw II Jagiello, founding the Jagiellonian dynasty and beginning the Christianization of Lithuania.

She helped fund the restoration of the Krakow Academy, later the Jagiellonian University, through jewellery donated and, under her will, sold to help finance it, helping revive an institution that became a major center of learning in Central Europe.

She died in 1399, about three and a half weeks after giving birth to a daughter who also died in infancy, four days before her, ending her direct line; she was canonized by the Catholic Church in 1997.
person/jadwiga.context: Jadwiga ruled Poland in Europe during the Medieval Period, and her marriage began the Polish-Lithuanian union. See Religion and Belief, Kinship and Society and War and Conflict.
person/jadwiga.observer: The Observer notes that Jadwiga's reign is remembered largely for a marriage alliance and a religious conversion she enabled rather than personal political acts, yet the union of Poland and Lithuania that resulted reshaped Central European power for centuries, an outsized consequence for a reign that ended before she turned thirty.
questions: How much personal agency did the ten-year-old Jadwiga have in the political decision to crown her as king, versus her regency council?

person/jan-van-eyck.title: Jan van Eyck
person/jan-van-eyck.summary: Jan van Eyck (born about 1380 or 1390, died 1441) was the leading painter of the Burgundian Netherlands and a founder of Early Netherlandish painting. He refined a method of thin, translucent oil glazes that let him paint light and texture with unprecedented realism.
facts: Van Eyck was probably born sometime around 1380 or 1390 near Maaseik, in present-day Belgian Limburg. Nothing is known of his training. He appears in records about 1422 at The Hague, working for John of Bavaria.

From 1425 he was court painter and valet de chambre to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, who sent him on confidential missions, including a trip to Portugal in 1428 to 1429 to paint Princess Isabella.
About 1430 he settled in Bruges. He completed the Ghent Altarpiece, begun by his brother Hubert, in 1432, and died in Bruges in July 1441.
He did not invent oil paint, as Vasari later claimed. He built up many thin, transparent glazes, and he often signed and dated his work, sometimes with the motto Als ich can ("As I can").
Key works include the Ghent Altarpiece (1432), the Arnolfini Portrait (1434) and the Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (about 1435).
He did not use the mathematical perspective being developed in Italy. He built space through observation of light and atmosphere.

The Ghent Altarpiece survived iconoclasm, fire and Napoleon's looters, was seized by the Nazis, and was recovered from an Austrian salt mine. A restoration begun in 2012 revealed the Lamb's strikingly human face in 2020.
person/jan-van-eyck.context: Van Eyck worked in Europe in the Medieval Period, at the time of the Renaissance. See Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/jan-van-eyck.observer: The Observer notes that a patron who pays for close detail is also buying status-signal, since a jewel-like surface shows that its owner can command rare materials and slow labour. The candles, fruit and mirrors link everyday objects to the meaning-engine, so the same careful looking serves both prestige and belief. That a whole technique was long credited to one man shows how a tool-lineage tends to be compressed into a single name. His role and his brother's on the Ghent Altarpiece is only partly recoverable.
questions: How much of the Ghent Altarpiece was painted by Hubert van Eyck rather than Jan?

person/jane-austen.title: Jane Austen
person/jane-austen.summary: Jane Austen (1775 to 1817) was an English novelist whose six completed novels of courtship, inheritance and class anxiety among the gentry remain among the most widely read in the language. All were published anonymously in her lifetime.
facts: Austen was born in 1775 in Steventon, Hampshire, the seventh of eight children of a country clergyman, in a family that encouraged reading, amateur theatre and writing.

Sense and Sensibility appeared in 1811, credited only to "A Lady", followed by Pride and Prejudice (1813), Mansfield Park (1814), Emma (1815) and, after her death, Northanger Abbey and Persuasion (1817).

Only close family knew of her authorship. She fell ill, probably with Addison's disease though the cause is debated, and died in 1817 at 41. Her authorship was publicly acknowledged in a biographical notice her brother attached to her last two novels.
She worked within a deliberately narrow social canvas, mainly the English gentry, courtship, income and inheritance, rather than the wider political events of her era.

Her distinctive technique is free indirect discourse: narrating in the third person while letting the prose absorb a character's own irony or blind spots, so the reader senses a character's error before the character does.
Her novels have remained continuously in print and are widely adapted for film, television and stage. Her reputation grew after her death rather than during her modest anonymous success.
person/jane-austen.context: Austen wrote in Europe in the Industrial Age, during the Napoleonic Wars, but kept to the gentry's household world. See Art and Ritual, Language and Writing and Kinship and Society.
person/jane-austen.observer: The Observer notes a body of fiction in which the kin-lattice, marriage, inheritance and income, is the whole plot, so that the machinery of who may marry whom and who inherits is made a subject of comedy rather than law. Her authorship was hidden while she lived, and her fame is a later assignment. The claim that she chose a narrow canvas over the wars of her age is an interpretation of her silence, and a reader could equally see the wars as absent because the household itself was her subject.
questions: What caused her final illness?

person/jayavarman-vii.title: Jayavarman VII
person/jayavarman-vii.summary: Jayavarman VII (about 1122 to about 1218) was king of the Khmer Empire from about 1181 until his death. He drove out Cham invaders who had sacked Angkor and then led a large building program that included Angkor Thom and the Bayon.
facts: Champa forces sacked Angkor in 1177. Jayavarman VII defeated them and was crowned about 1181; his birth and death years are estimates.
Khmer forces later brought parts of Champa under Khmer control.
He was a Mahayana Buddhist, while most earlier Khmer rulers had favored Hindu cults.
His projects include Angkor Thom, the Bayon with its towers carved with large faces, Ta Prohm (dedicated to his mother) and Preah Khan (dedicated to his father).
An inscription of 1186 at Ta Prohm credits him with 102 hospitals; the figure comes from the king's own inscriptions.
The faces on the Bayon towers are variously read as a Buddhist deity, the king, or both.
person/jayavarman-vii.context: Jayavarman VII ruled the Khmer Empire from Angkor in Southeast Asia during the Medieval Period and fought Champa. See Religion and Belief, War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
person/jayavarman-vii.observer: The Observer notes that Jayavarman VII took power after Angkor was sacked from outside and answered with building on an unusual scale: temples for his parents, hospitals, and a walled city whose towers carry giant faces. His inscriptions present these works as merit-making by a Buddhist king, which also served as a claim to legitimacy. The labor behind them appears in the record as the king's gift, and the workers are almost invisible. A specialist could argue that the program strained Angkor's resources, which would weaken a reading of it as simply benevolent.
questions: Whom do the faces of the Bayon depict?

person/jeong-seon.title: Jeong Seon
person/jeong-seon.summary: Jeong Seon (1676 to 1759), pen name Gyeomjae, was a Korean painter of the Joseon dynasty who transformed landscape painting by depicting the real scenery of Korea instead of imagined Chinese scenery. His "true-view landscape" (jingyeong sansuhwa) expressed a growing pride in Korean culture.
facts: Jeong Seon was born in 1676 in Hanyang (modern Seoul), into a scholarly family of modest means. His father died when he was young. He trained in painting and in Neo-Confucian learning.
Through recommendations he held government posts, including county magistrate at Hayang and Yangcheon, and rose to high official rank in old age.
He lived near Mount Inwang in Seoul. His friend the poet Yi Byeong-yeon exchanged poems and paintings with him for decades.
In 1711 and 1712 he travelled to the Diamond Mountains (Geumgangsan), and the albums he made there made his name. He died in 1759 at 83.

For centuries Korean painters had followed Chinese models. He painted the actual scenery of Korea and invented his own brushstrokes: sharp vertical strokes for granite peaks and soft wet dots for forested earth mountains.
He often combined a bird's-eye view with exaggeration. His paintings are not maps but expressions of the experience of real places.
Two works, Geumgang jeondo and Inwang jesaekdo, are National Treasures of South Korea. Kim Hong-do and Sim Sa-jeong followed him, and the Gyeomjae Jeong Seon Art Museum opened in Seoul in 2009.
person/jeong-seon.context: Jeong Seon worked in Joseon Korea in East Asia during the Early Modern Period. See Art and Ritual.
person/jeong-seon.observer: The Observer notes a shift in whose mountains count. For centuries Korean painters followed Chinese models of idealised scenery, and Jeong Seon painted the granite of the actual peninsula. The change was carried by a network of friends who exchanged poems and paintings, and it expressed a pride in local place, a story-glue of landscape. Because the paintings are expressions rather than surveys, "true view" should be read as an intention, not a measurement of the terrain.
questions: How closely do the true-view paintings follow the real landscape?

person/johannes-gutenberg.title: Johannes Gutenberg
person/johannes-gutenberg.summary: Johannes Gutenberg (about 1400 to 1468) was a German metalworker who developed a movable-type printing press in Mainz around 1440 and printed the Gutenberg Bible about 1455.
facts: He combined metal type, oil-based ink, and a press adapted from wine-making.
The 42-line Bible is the earliest major book printed from movable type in Europe.
He faced financial difficulties and lost control of his workshop to a creditor.
Printing spread rapidly across Europe within decades.
person/johannes-gutenberg.context: See Movable-Type Printing Press. Gutenberg's work supported the Scientific Revolution and religious reform.
person/johannes-gutenberg.observer: The Observer notes that Gutenberg's innovation made memory-outsourcing cheap and copyable. Ideas began to travel faster than any authority could suppress them.

person/johannes-vermeer.title: Johannes Vermeer
person/johannes-vermeer.summary: Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675) was a painter of Delft in the Dutch Republic. About 35 paintings are accepted as his, mostly quiet interiors lit by daylight from a window. Almost forgotten for 200 years after his death, he is now among the most famous painters in the world.
facts: Vermeer was baptised in Delft on 31 October 1632. His father was a silk weaver who also dealt in art and ran an inn. Nothing is known of Vermeer's training.

In 1653 he married Catharina Bolnes, a Catholic from a wealthier family, and probably converted. The same year he joined Delft's Guild of St Luke, which later elected him one of its leaders several times.
The couple lived with Catharina's mother and had 15 children, 11 of whom survived. He also worked as an art dealer, and his slow output was bought largely by one local patron, Pieter van Ruijven.
In 1672, the Dutch Republic's "Disaster Year", France invaded and the art market collapsed. He died in 1675, aged 43, leaving his family deep in debt.

He used costly natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli, even in shadows. Key works include The Milkmaid (about 1657 to 1658), View of Delft (about 1660 to 1661) and Girl with a Pearl Earring (about 1665).
Some features of his paintings have led scholars to argue that he used a camera obscura. The question remains debated.

In the 1860s the critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger rediscovered him. In the 1940s Han van Meegeren sold a fake Vermeer to Hermann Göring. A 2023 Rijksmuseum exhibition of 28 of his works sold out within days.
person/johannes-vermeer.context: Vermeer worked in Delft in Europe during the Early Modern Period. See Art and Ritual.
person/johannes-vermeer.observer: The Observer notes that the calm of the pictures sits beside a household of 15 children, debt and a collapsing art market, so the serenity was made under pressure. That he was forgotten for two centuries and then rediscovered shows that fame is assigned by later readers. Whether he used a camera obscura is a question about a tool-lineage in painting that remains unsettled, and forgeries such as van Meegeren's show how high the status-signal of his name has become.
questions: Did Vermeer use a camera obscura, and if so how?

person/john-curtin.title: John Curtin
person/john-curtin.summary: John Curtin (1885 to 1945) was Prime Minister of Australia from 1941 to 1945, leading the country through the Pacific war against Japan during the Second World War.
facts: A former journalist and trade unionist who had opposed conscription during the First World War, he became Labor Party leader in 1935 and prime minister in October 1941.

After Japan entered the war in December 1941 and bombed Darwin in February 1942, he redirected Australian forces from the European theatre and, over British objections, recalled Australian troops from the Middle East to defend against Japanese advance.
He committed Australia more closely to the United States for wartime defense, stating in December 1941 that Australia looked to America "free of any pangs" about its traditional ties to Britain.

He introduced wartime economic controls and expanded the Australian government's role in social welfare, but died in office in July 1945, weeks before Japan's surrender, worn down by the strain of the war years.
person/john-curtin.context: John Curtin led Australia, in Oceania, through the Pacific War during the Industrial Age. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/john-curtin.observer: The Observer notes that Curtin's turn toward the United States marked a lasting realignment of Australian strategic dependence away from Britain, made under the pressure of direct attack rather than as a considered peacetime choice. That a leader who had opposed conscription in one war ended up directing total national mobilization in the next is a reminder that circumstance can override a leader's earlier convictions.
questions: How much of Australia's postwar alignment with the United States was set irreversibly by Curtin's wartime decisions, versus later Cold War pressures?

person/jose-marti.title: José Martí
person/jose-marti.summary: José Martí (1853 to 1895) was a Cuban poet, journalist and organizer who founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party in 1892 and helped launch the 1895 war of independence against Spain. He was killed in one of its first battles.
facts: Martí was born in Havana on 28 January 1853. Arrested at 16 over a letter criticizing a schoolmate who joined the Spanish army, he was sentenced to six years' hard labor and deported to Spain in 1871. He later lived in Mexico, Guatemala, Venezuela and, from 1880, mainly New York.
He published Ismaelillo (1882), Versos sencillos (1891) and the essay "Nuestra América" (1891), which argued that Latin American countries should govern from knowledge of their own peoples.
In 1892 he founded the Cuban Revolutionary Party and its newspaper Patria, arguing for a republic open to all races and against United States expansion into Cuba.
He landed in eastern Cuba on 11 April 1895 and was killed at Dos Ríos on 19 May in his first engagement. Cuba became formally independent in 1902, under limits set by the United States.
Both the Cuban government and Cuban exile groups have since claimed him as a symbol.
person/jose-marti.context: Martí worked in the Caribbean and Atlantic World during the Industrial Age, in the last years of Spanish rule in the Americas, echoing Simón Bolívar and the Latin American Wars of Independence. See Language and Writing and War and Conflict.
person/jose-marti.observer: The Observer notes that a nation not yet in existence was first assembled as words: poems, newspaper articles and speeches among exiles. It was a story-glue made in mark-code before any claim-line had been drawn. A specialist could argue that his own plans fit the record less closely than the later statues do, which would weaken a reading of him as the origin of Cuban identity rather than one of its shapers.
questions: Which positions later attributed to him are in his own writings?
What did he plan for the republic after independence?

person/jose-maria-velasco.title: José María Velasco
person/jose-maria-velasco.summary: José María Velasco (6 July 1840 to 26 August 1912) was the most important Mexican painter of the 19th century, known for panoramic views of the Valley of Mexico. He was also a trained naturalist who illustrated scientific publications on botany, zoology and geology.
facts: Velasco was born in Temascalcingo, in the State of Mexico. His family moved to Mexico City in 1849. In 1858 he entered the Academy of San Carlos, where the Italian painter Eugenio Landesio taught him to observe nature closely and paint outdoors. He also studied botany, zoology, anatomy, physics and mathematics.
In 1877 he succeeded Landesio as professor of landscape painting. Among his students was Diego Rivera.
He worked as a scientific illustrator for the National Museum and on expeditions, and painted archaeological sites such as Teotihuacan.

He won a medal at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1889 and exhibited at the 1893 Chicago World's Columbian Exposition. One view of the Valley of Mexico was given to Pope Leo XIII and is now in the Vatican Museums.

He worked from outdoor sketches to large studio compositions. His panoramas set a detailed foreground of cacti and rocks against a luminous distance, and often include railways, bridges and haciendas alongside nature and ruins.
Key works include The Valley of Mexico from the Santa Isabel Mountain Range (1875), The Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan (1878) and The Curved Bridge over the Metlac Ravine (1881).
He died in Mexico City during the early years of the Mexican Revolution. His views record lakes and open plains since swallowed by Mexico City. The Museo José María Velasco in Toluca opened in 1992.
person/jose-maria-velasco.context: Velasco worked in Mesoamerica in the Industrial Age, painting Teotihuacan and the valley around former Tenochtitlan, and died during the Mexican Revolution. See Art and Ritual and Science.
person/jose-maria-velasco.observer: The Observer notes a landscape painter who was also a trained naturalist, so that one picture served as an image of a nation and a catalogue of plants, rocks and light. After independence a country needed a visual identity, and a panorama of its valley supplied one, a story-glue in paint. Because the lakes and plains he recorded have been built over, the paintings have since become a record of a place that no longer exists, a reading he did not necessarily intend.
questions: How much of his composed panoramas is observation, and how much idealisation?

person/jose-rizal.title: José Rizal
person/jose-rizal.summary: José Rizal (1861 to 1896) was a Filipino physician, writer and reformer whose novels criticized Spanish colonial rule. Spanish authorities executed him in Manila on 30 December 1896, and he is regarded as a national hero of the Philippines.
facts: Rizal was born on 19 June 1861 in Calamba, in the Philippines. He studied in Manila, Madrid, Paris and Heidelberg and became an eye doctor.
He wrote the novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and El Filibusterismo (1891), which portrayed abuses by Spanish friars and officials; the colonial authorities banned them.
In 1892 he founded La Liga Filipina, a reform society, and was exiled to Dapitan on Mindanao, where he practiced medicine and taught until 1896.

The Philippine Revolution began in August 1896. Rizal, who had volunteered as a doctor in Cuba, was arrested on his way there, brought back to Manila and convicted of rebellion. He had said he opposed an armed uprising at that time.
He was shot by firing squad on 30 December 1896, aged 35. Before his death he wrote a poem now known as "Mi último adiós."
person/jose-rizal.context: Rizal wrote in Southeast Asia and Europe during the Industrial Age, as Spain's colony in the Philippines, tied to the world since the Manila Galleon Trade, moved toward revolution. See Language and Writing and Science.
person/jose-rizal.observer: The Observer notes that Rizal used the novel, a foreign literary form, as a mark-code weapon: fiction gave readers a shared picture of abuses that formal reports could not. His execution turned a reformer into a symbol for revolutionaries who had taken a path he had not endorsed, showing how a story-glue for a new nation can be built from a person's death. The reading would weaken if fuller records showed he was closer to the revolutionaries than his statements suggest.
questions: How close was his connection to the revolutionary movement that used his name?

person/joao-iii.title: João III
person/joao-iii.summary: João III (1502 to 1557) was King of Portugal from 1521 to 1557, presiding over the height of Portugal's Asian trading empire while also introducing the Inquisition and formal colonization of Brazil.
facts: Under his reign Portuguese trading posts and fortresses across the Indian Ocean, from East Africa to Goa, Malacca and Macau, reached their fullest extent, built on the routes opened by earlier explorers such as Vasco da Gama.

He introduced the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, targeting Jewish converts (New Christians) suspected of secretly practicing Judaism, at the urging of factions at his court and with eventual papal approval.
He divided Brazil into hereditary captaincies from 1534 to encourage settlement and defense of the colony, a system that had mixed results and was later partly replaced by direct royal government.

He was a patron of Portuguese scholarship, moving the university at Lisbon to Coimbra in 1537, but the enormous cost of maintaining the Asian trading empire strained the crown's finances by the end of his reign.
person/joao-iii.context: João III ruled Portugal in Europe during the Early Modern Period, overseeing its trading empire and the colonization of Brazil. See Trade and Economy and Religion and Belief.
person/joao-iii.observer: The Observer notes that João III's reign shows a single government running two very different colonial projects at once, a trade-post empire in Asia built on existing networks and a settlement colony in Brazil built from the ground up, each with different costs and consequences that later history would treat very differently.
questions: How much did the financial strain of maintaining the Asian trading posts contribute to Portugal's later loss of influence there to the Dutch and English?

person/kamehameha-i.title: Kamehameha I
person/kamehameha-i.summary: Kamehameha I (about 1750 to 1819) was a chief of Hawaiʻi Island who united the Hawaiian Islands under one rule by 1810, founding the Kingdom of Hawaiʻi, whose last monarch was Liliuokalani.
facts: Kamehameha was born at Kohala on Hawaiʻi Island. Estimates of his birth year range from 1736 to 1761. He died on 8 May 1819, though some sources say 14 May.

After his uncle, the ruler Kalaniʻōpuʻu, died in 1782, he became guardian of the war god Kūkaʻilimoku and defeated his cousin Kīwalaʻō at the Battle of Mokuʻōhai, gaining Hawaiʻi Island after years of war.
He used Western firearms and cannon and advisers such as John Young and Isaac Davis. In 1795 he invaded Oʻahu, and at Nuʻuanu hundreds of defenders were driven over the Pali cliff.
In 1810 Kauaʻi and Niʻihau came under his authority by negotiation with their ruler Kaumualiʻi, who stayed on as a tributary king.
The Law of the Splintered Paddle (Māmalahoe Kānāwai), protecting noncombatants, is said to come from a 1782 incident in which fishermen struck him with a paddle.
His son Liholiho succeeded him as Kamehameha II. His burial place was hidden by custom and is unknown.
person/kamehameha-i.context: Kamehameha I lived in Oceania among the Polynesians, whose voyagers had settled Hawaiʻi centuries earlier in the Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific. The kingdom he founded ended with Liliuokalani. See War and Conflict and Trade and Economy.
person/kamehameha-i.observer: The Observer notes that a chief built one state by joining an old priestly and war lineage to imported gunpowder, choosing tribute over killing the last rival ruler. His hidden grave was a grief-rite that also protected his bones from rivals. A specialist could argue the unification also depended on Western trade and on divisions among his opponents, which would weaken a reading of the outcome as his design alone.
questions: When was he born, and how did his age shape his own accounts of his rise?
How much of the 1810 unification was negotiation, and how much the threat of force?

person/kate-sheppard.title: Kate Sheppard
person/kate-sheppard.summary: Kate Sheppard (1848 to 1934) was an English-born campaigner who led the movement for women's suffrage in New Zealand. The Electoral Act of 1893 made New Zealand the first self-governing country in which women voted in national elections.
facts: Sheppard was born on 10 March 1848 in Liverpool, England, and emigrated to New Zealand, arriving in 1869. She died in Christchurch on 13 July 1934.
From 1887 she was national superintendent for franchise and legislation of the Women's Christian Temperance Union, which made votes for women a central aim.
Petitions to Parliament carried about 10,000 signatures in 1891, about 20,000 in 1892 and 31,872 in 1893, the largest petition presented to Parliament until then.
The Governor signed the Electoral Act on 19 September 1893, and women voted for the first time in the election of 28 November 1893.
The Act gave the vote to women of all races, including Māori women in the Māori electorates, but women could not stand for Parliament until 1919.
Her portrait has been on the New Zealand ten-dollar note since 1991.
person/kate-sheppard.context: Kate Sheppard worked in Oceania during the Industrial Age, as part of the international Women's Suffrage Movements. See Maori and Kinship and Society.
person/kate-sheppard.observer: The Observer notes that a claim-line around who counted as a citizen was moved by counting, a temperance network turning shared conviction into signatures a legislature could tally. The line moved in steps, with the vote won in 1893 and the right to stand only in 1919. A specialist could argue the vote came from many organizers and sympathetic politicians besides her, which would weaken a reading that centers one person.
questions: How much of the 1893 result owed to her leadership, and how much to other organizers?
How did Māori women take part in the campaign?

person/katsushika-hokusai.title: Katsushika Hokusai
person/katsushika-hokusai.summary: Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849) was a Japanese ukiyo-e artist from Edo, creator of The Great Wave off Kanagawa. He produced paintings, book illustrations and, in his seventies, the landscape print series that made him world-famous.
facts: Hokusai was born in 1760 in the Katsushika district of Edo (modern Tokyo). As a teenager he worked in a lending library and trained as a woodblock carver. About 18 he entered the studio of Katsukawa Shunshō.

He changed his artistic name more than 30 times and is said to have moved house more than 90 times. He lived in poverty for much of his life. His daughter Katsushika Ōi became a fine painter and assisted him in his old age.
In 1814 he began publishing the Hokusai Manga, fifteen volumes of sketches. About 1830 to 1832 he designed Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, which includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa (about 1831).

In the postscript to One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji (1834) he wrote that nothing he drew before age 70 was worth noticing. He died in Edo on 10 May 1849, at 88, reportedly saying that with five more years he could have become a true painter.

Ukiyo-e was a collaborative art: he drew the design, specialist carvers cut it into blocks, one for each colour, and printers pressed the paper by hand. The Fuji series used the newly imported Prussian blue pigment.
He learned Western perspective from Dutch prints available in Japan and combined it with Japanese flat colour and strong design.

After Japan opened to trade in the 1850s he became a sensation in Europe. Monet, Degas, Van Gogh and Cassatt learned from him, and Debussy put The Great Wave on the cover of La Mer. The 1,000-yen note issued in 2024 carries the wave, and the Sumida Hokusai Museum opened in Tokyo in 2016.
person/katsushika-hokusai.context: Hokusai worked in Edo under the Tokugawa Shogunate in East Asia, in the Industrial Age. See Art and Ritual and Trade and Economy.
person/katsushika-hokusai.observer: The Observer notes that the famous print is a workshop's output, a designer's drawing multiplied by carvers and printers into thousands of impressions, so the "artwork" is a process rather than a single object. Its blue arrived by exchange-web, and its European fame came by the same webs decades later. The stories of 30 names, 90 houses and a deathbed remark present an artist who narrated his own maturation, and part of that narrative is reported rather than documented.
questions: How large was Katsushika Ōi's contribution to his late work?

person/khadija-bint-khuwaylid.title: Khadija bint Khuwaylid
person/khadija-bint-khuwaylid.summary: Khadija bint Khuwaylid (about 555 to 619) was a merchant of Mecca and the first wife of Muhammad. Her dates and many details come from Muslim biographies written more than a century after her death.
facts: Khadija belonged to the Quraysh tribe of Mecca and, according to tradition, financed trading caravans to Syria and hired agents to lead them.
Tradition says Muhammad led one of her caravans and that she proposed marriage, about 595. Accounts differ on her age then, and a common figure is 40.
Muslim tradition holds that she was the first person to accept Muhammad's message after his first revelation, about 610.
Tradition names four daughters, including Fatima, and sons who died young.
She died about 619, shortly before Muhammad's move to Medina in 622, a year remembered as the Year of Sorrow.
The earliest biographies, by Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Saʿd, were written in the 8th and 9th centuries.
person/khadija-bint-khuwaylid.context: Khadija's life falls before the Rise of Islam and is closely tied to Muhammad in the Arabian Peninsula of the Medieval Period. See Trade and Economy, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
person/khadija-bint-khuwaylid.observer: The Observer notes that early Muslim biographers, writing more than a century later, describe a woman who held capital, employed a man, proposed to him, and then funded and comforted the first movement around him. It is hard to say whether the record preserves her role or shapes it to serve later ideals. Descent through her daughter Fatima became a status-signal for many later families, so her kin-lattice carried weight long after her death. The reading would weaken if the tradition simplified her marriages and ages.
questions: How much of the early account of her wealth and trade is independently supported?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Muhammad reportedly managed one of Khadija's trading caravans to Syria, after which she proposed marriage to him around 595 CE, with her age at the time often given as about 40 [Wikipedia on Khadija bint Khuwaylid]

2026-09-27: Following Muhammad's first revelation around 610 CE, Khadija is held by Muslim tradition to have been the first person to accept his message [Wikipedia on Khadija bint Khuwaylid; Britannica on Khadijah]

2026-09-27: Khadija died in November 619, a year Muhammad called the Year of Sorrow, roughly three years before the Hijra to Medina in 622 [Wikipedia on Khadija bint Khuwaylid; Britannica on Khadijah]

person/knud-rasmussen.title: Knud Rasmussen
person/knud-rasmussen.summary: Knud Rasmussen (1879 to 1933) was a Danish-Greenlandic explorer and ethnographer who recorded Inuit oral traditions and led the Fifth Thule Expedition (1921 to 1924), a dog-sled journey from Greenland across Arctic Canada to Alaska.
facts: Knud Rasmussen was born on 7 June 1879 in Jakobshavn (Ilulissat), Greenland, to a Danish missionary father and a mother of part Greenlandic Inuit descent, and grew up speaking Greenlandic.
In 1910 he and Peter Freuchen founded the Thule Trading Station at Cape York in northwest Greenland, which helped fund his expeditions.

On the Fifth Thule Expedition he traveled with Greenlandic Inuit companions across northern Canada to Alaska. The expedition's archaeologist, Therkel Mathiassen, excavated sites that led to the identification of the Thule culture.
He collected songs, stories and accounts of belief from the Iglulik and other Inuit groups, and wrote Across Arctic America (1927).
He fell ill on the Seventh Thule Expedition and died in Copenhagen on 21 December 1933.
person/knud-rasmussen.context: Rasmussen's work covered the peoples described in Inuit and the Thule Expansion, across Arctic coasts near Beringia, in Siberia and the Arctic during the Industrial Age. See Science, Language and Writing and Trade and Economy.
person/knud-rasmussen.observer: The Observer notes that Rasmussen stood between two kin-lattices, Danish and Greenlandic, and that speaking Greenlandic from childhood let him record songs and accounts an outside visitor might have missed. His route followed a chain of related Inuit communities, a reminder that a language and kin network can run across lines drawn by states. His records depend on Danish trade and expedition funding, so they reflect his interests and informants as well as the communities. Inuit scholars could argue that Inuit-produced accounts deserve more weight than his volumes, which would weaken any reading that treats them as the standard record.
questions: How do Inuit accounts of the same events compare with his versions?

person/kristina-of-sweden.title: Kristina of Sweden
person/kristina-of-sweden.summary: Kristina (1626 to 1689) was Queen of Sweden from 1632 to 1654, known for her patronage of scholars and the arts, her unexpected abdication, and her secret conversion to Catholicism in a firmly Protestant kingdom.
facts: She became queen at age five after her father Gustavus Adolphus died in battle, ruling under a regency until she assumed full power in 1644.
She invited scholars including Rene Descartes to her court in Stockholm; Descartes died there in 1650, reportedly worn down by the early-morning hours she kept for their lessons.

She abdicated the throne in 1654 in favor of her cousin, and after leaving Sweden she converted to Catholicism in secret in Brussels in December 1654, a decision scandalous in Lutheran Sweden that she announced publicly in 1655.
She spent most of her later life in Rome under the pope's protection, becoming a prominent patron of music and art, and was one of very few women buried in St. Peter's Basilica.
person/kristina-of-sweden.context: Kristina ruled Sweden in Europe during the Early Modern Period before her abdication and conversion. See Religion and Belief, Science and Art and Ritual.
person/kristina-of-sweden.observer: The Observer notes that Kristina gave up one of Europe's more secure thrones for a religious conviction she could not act on while she held it, a rare case of a monarch choosing personal belief over political power outright rather than being forced from office by rivals or war.
questions: How much of her abdication was driven by religious conviction alone, versus a broader discomfort with the constraints of Swedish court life and expectations of marriage?

person/kupe.title: Kupe
person/kupe.summary: Kupe is a legendary Polynesian navigator credited in Maori oral tradition with being the first to reach and name Aotearoa (New Zealand); no fixed historical date can be assigned to him.
facts: Traditions describe Kupe sailing from the ancestral homeland Hawaiki, in some versions pursuing the giant octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi, and reaching the North Island of New Zealand.
He is credited with naming numerous coastal landmarks, several of which are still used today, and with returning to Hawaiki afterward to describe the land he had found.

Different iwi (tribal) traditions place him at varying points, and 19th- and 20th-century European writers synthesized these into a single traditional date of roughly 925 CE (the orthodox version tied to S. Percy Smith; other sources give about 900 to 1200 CE) that many historians now treat with caution.

No archaeological or written record fixes Kupe's voyage; the earliest confirmed archaeological evidence for human settlement of New Zealand dates to around the 13th century CE, later than most traditional accounts imply.
person/kupe.context: Kupe belongs to the oral traditions of the Maori, part of the wider spread of the Polynesians across Oceania during the Medieval Period. See Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
person/kupe.observer: The Observer notes that Kupe functions less as a single dateable person than as a way of organizing a founding story: giving named ancestors, named canoes and named landmarks to a settlement process that archaeology now dates centuries later than the traditional accounts suggest. That gap does not make the tradition false, but it means the story and the settlement record answer different questions.
questions: How much of the Kupe tradition reflects a single voyage rather than a composite of several early journeys?

2026-09-27: Oral histories describe Kupe pursuing the great octopus Te Wheke-a-Muturangi, which in one telling he destroys in Cook Strait, and naming places such as Matiu (Somes Island) and Makaro (Ward Island), with the names associated with Kupe having endured. [Wikipedia on Kupe]

2026-09-27: In the so-called orthodox version tied to S. Percy Smith, Kupe arrives in New Zealand in 925 CE and on returning to Hawaiki tells of his adventures and persuades others to migrate, but the status of that version is contested because earlier attested tribal traditions make Kupe a contemporary of the other founding canoes. [Wikipedia on Kupe]

2026-09-27: There are no human remains, artefacts or structures confidently dated earlier than the Kaharoa Tephra deposited around 1314 CE, and mitochondrial DNA evidence suggests Polynesians first settled New Zealand between 1250 and 1300. [Wikipedia on History of New Zealand]

2026-09-27: The early European synthesis of Maori oral tradition that placed Kupe's discovery centuries before a single great fleet has, since the late 20th century, been increasingly relegated to the realm of myth. [Wikipedia on History of New Zealand]

person/lady-six-sky.title: Lady Six Sky
person/lady-six-sky.summary: Lady Six Sky (Wak Chanil Ajaw; active 682 to 741 CE) was a Maya noblewoman from Dos Pilas who arrived at Naranjo in 682 and effectively ruled the city for decades, restoring it after a period of defeat.
facts: She was a daughter of the Dos Pilas king B'alaj Chan K'awiil, part of a network of the powerful city of Calakmul's allies against its rival Tikal.
Naranjo's royal line had been broken after a defeat by Caracol, and Lady Six Sky was installed there in 682, apparently to re-establish the dynasty.

Monuments record her overseeing military campaigns and presiding over her young son K'ahk' Tiliw Chan Chaahk's accession in 693, after which she continued to appear on inscriptions as a ruling figure into the 700s.

She never took the full royal title used by male kings of Naranjo, and continued to use the emblem glyph of her home city Dos Pilas throughout her life, so her exact formal status is debated by epigraphers.
person/lady-six-sky.context: Lady Six Sky's career took place among the Maya city-states of Mesoamerica during the Medieval Period, within the wider rivalry between Calakmul and Tikal for regional dominance. See War and Conflict, Kinship and Society and Religion and Belief.
person/lady-six-sky.observer: The Observer notes that Lady Six Sky held real power at Naranjo for decades while never claiming the title that would have named her a king in her own right, a gap between practice and title that Maya inscriptions do not explain. Reading her as a ruling queen assumes that authority and title track together; the monuments suggest they did not always.
questions: Did Lady Six Sky rule in her own right, or as an unusually powerful regent for her son?

2026-09-27: She was the daughter of B'alaj Chan K'awiil, king of Dos Pilas [Wikipedia on Lady Six Sky]

2026-09-27: Lady Six Sky died in 741, given in the Lady Six Sky article as 10 or 11 February 741 [Wikipedia on Lady Six Sky; Wikipedia on Naranjo, Guatemala]

person/laozi.title: Laozi
person/laozi.summary: Laozi (Lao Tzu, "Old Master") is the traditional author of the Daodejing and a founding figure of Daoism, said to have lived in the 6th century BCE. Whether he was a single historical person is disputed.
facts: Laozi is traditionally placed in the 6th century BCE, in the time of Confucius. The date is uncertain and no date of death is known.
The historian Sima Qian, writing about 100 BCE, identifies him as Li Er, keeper of archives at the Zhou court, and also lists other men who might have been meant, so the uncertainty was already old.
Sima Qian's account says he met Confucius, then left the Zhou domain to the west and wrote the text at the Hangu Pass at the request of the gatekeeper Yin Xi. This account is traditional.

The Daodejing has about 5,000 Chinese characters in 81 short chapters. Its earliest excavated versions, from Guodian (about 300 BCE) and Mawangdui (tomb sealed 168 BCE), fit the view of most scholars that the text took shape in the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE.
Later religious Daoism honored him as a deity, Laojun, and the Tang dynasty's imperial family, named Li, claimed him as an ancestor.
person/laozi.context: Laozi is a figure of the Axial Age in East Asia during the Iron Age, often paired with Confucius. See Religion and Belief and Language and Writing.
person/laozi.observer: The Observer notes that a book was attached to a person, and the person to a place and a story, a pattern in which the text arrives first and the biography follows. Whether one man wrote it matters less to its history than what later people did with the figure: the Tang emperors used descent from him as a story-glue for their claim to rule. A single well-dated author would weaken this reading, while evidence of several hands over generations would strengthen it.
questions: Was there a single author, or was the Daodejing assembled over generations?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Laozi is traditionally placed in the 6th century BCE, though some scholars date him to the 4th century BCE, and modern scholars remain divided over his identity, dates and relationship to the received text [Wikipedia on Laozi]

2026-09-27: Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, completed c. 91 BCE, identifies Laozi as Li Er, keeper of the archives at the royal Zhou court, says he met Confucius, and also offers other candidates such as Lao Laizi and a later court astrologer Lao Dan [Wikipedia on Laozi]

2026-09-27: The Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) has 81 short chapters and roughly 5,162 to 5,450 Chinese characters, and scholars broadly agree the text emerged in the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE, with most seeing it as a compilation rather than one author's work [Wikipedia on Tao Te Ching]

2026-09-27: The oldest known versions of the Daodejing are the Guodian bamboo slips (buried around 300 BCE), while the Mawangdui silk texts come from a tomb dated to 168 BCE [Wikipedia on Tao Te Ching]
2026-09-27: Laozi came to be identified with Laojun, a divine manifestation of the Dao, and the Li family emperors of the Tang dynasty traced their descent to Laozi [Wikipedia on Laozi]

person/lautaro.title: Lautaro
person/lautaro.summary: Lautaro (about 1534 to 1557) was a Mapuche toqui, or war leader (described at Tucapel as a vice toqui under the supreme toqui Caupolicán), who organized effective resistance to Spanish conquest in what is now southern Chile, after years spent as a captured servant in the Spanish camp.
facts: As a young captive, he served the Spanish conquistador Pedro de Valdivia and observed Spanish tactics, horsemanship and weapons before escaping back to his people.
He introduced cavalry tactics, relay messenger systems and coordinated ambushes to Mapuche warfare, adapting methods he had learned from the Spanish.

In December 1553 his forces, serving under the supreme toqui Caupolicán, defeated a Spanish column at the Battle of Tucapel, where Valdivia was captured and killed (sources differ on the details of his death), a major blow to the early Spanish conquest of Chile.
He was killed in a surprise Spanish attack on his camp at the Mataquito River in April 1557, ending a campaign that had held Spanish expansion south of the Bio-Bio River in check for years.
person/lautaro.context: Lautaro led Mapuche resistance in the Andes region during the Early Modern Period, part of the broader pattern of Indigenous resistance to Spanish colonization in the Americas. See War and Conflict.
person/lautaro.observer: The Observer notes that Lautaro's effectiveness came directly from his captivity: the same Spanish camp that used him as forced labor also taught him, inadvertently, how to defeat Spanish armies. The Mapuche remained unconquered by Spain for the rest of the colonial period, a rare outcome in the Americas that his early campaigns helped establish.
questions: How much of Lautaro's tactical innovation was his own, versus already circulating among Mapuche leaders resisting the Spanish?

2026-09-27: As a boy Lautaro was captured by the Spanish and forced into servitude as Pedro de Valdivia's personal servant, and he escaped after about three years in captivity [Wikipedia on Lautaro]
2026-09-27: The Battle of Tucapel was fought on 25 December 1553, and Valdivia was captured and killed, although the sources differ on how he died [Wikipedia on Battle of Tucapel]

person/leo-tolstoy.title: Leo Tolstoy
person/leo-tolstoy.summary: Leo Tolstoy (1828 to 1910) was a Russian novelist, author of the realist epics War and Peace and Anna Karenina. A religious crisis in the second half of his life turned him toward shorter fiction and writing on faith, mortality and nonviolence that influenced Gandhi.
facts: Tolstoy was born in 1828 into an aristocratic family at Yasnaya Polyana, the estate south of Moscow he inherited and managed for most of his life. He served briefly as an army officer in the Crimean War.
In the 1860s and 1870s he wrote War and Peace (1869) and Anna Karenina (1877), and founded a school for the children on his estate.

After Anna Karenina he underwent a spiritual crisis, described in A Confession. He rejected the Russian Orthodox Church, embraced an ascetic, pacifist reading of Christian ethics and increasingly disowned his earlier fiction as morally frivolous.
His later works include The Death of Ivan Ilyich (1886), The Kreutzer Sonata (1889) and Resurrection (1899), shorter, starker and more didactic than the novels.
War and Peace argues in long digressions that the forces driving historical events lay far beyond the control of any single general or emperor.
His writing on nonviolent resistance to evil directly influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who corresponded with him near the end of his life.
He died in 1910 of pneumonia at a remote railway station, after collapsing on a flight from his estate. Yasnaya Polyana is preserved as a museum.
person/leo-tolstoy.context: Tolstoy wrote in the Russian Empire, in Europe, during the Industrial Age, and his ethics passed through Mahatma Gandhi into later traditions of nonviolence. See Art and Ritual, Language and Writing and Religion and Belief.
person/leo-tolstoy.observer: The Observer notes a writer who argued that history is driven by forces beyond any general or emperor, then in later life disowned his own fiction and preached nonviolence, so that one person tested two accounts of what moves people. The line from Tolstoy to Gandhi is a meaning-engine's ethics passing from hand to hand by letter, and from there into political movements. The flight from the estate and the death at a railway station make an ending that invites retelling, so the account of his last days deserves the same care as any other late-life narrative.
questions: How much of his later disavowal of his own novels was reasoned, and how much a crisis?

person/leonardo-da-vinci.title: Leonardo da Vinci
person/leonardo-da-vinci.summary: Leonardo da Vinci (15 April 1452 to 2 May 1519) was an Italian painter, engineer and anatomist. He left few finished paintings, with counts differing but fewer than 25 attributed major works, some of them unfinished, including the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and thousands of notebook pages of studies.
facts: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 near Vinci in Tuscany, the illegitimate son of a notary, Ser Piero, and a young woman named Caterina. He was apprenticed in Florence to Andrea del Verrocchio.
About 1482 he moved to Milan. In a letter to Duke Ludovico Sforza he stressed his skills as a military engineer before his art. In Milan he painted The Last Supper.
After the French invaded Milan in 1499 he moved between Mantua, Venice and Florence, worked briefly as a military engineer for Cesare Borgia, and in Florence began the Mona Lisa.

In 1516 King Francis I invited him to France and gave him the manor of Clos Lucé near Amboise. He died there on 2 May 1519. His pupil Francesco Melzi inherited his paintings, tools, library and personal effects, and by tradition his notebooks.
His notebooks hold thousands of pages of drawings and mirror-writing, with studies of anatomy, flight, hydraulics and optics. He dissected corpses to understand muscles and bones.

He pioneered sfumato, soft modelling without hard outlines. Key works include the Virgin of the Rocks (about 1483 to 1493, sources differ), Lady with an Ermine (about 1489 to 1491), Vitruvian Man (about 1485 to 1490, sources differ), The Last Supper (about 1495 to 1498) and the Mona Lisa (about 1503 to 1519).
His experiments with materials sometimes failed: The Last Supper began to decay within decades.
The Codex Leicester was bought by Bill Gates in 1994. In 2017 the Salvator Mundi, attributed to Leonardo, sold for $450 million, a record for a painting; its attribution remains disputed.
person/leonardo-da-vinci.context: Leonardo worked in Europe in the Medieval Period, during the Renaissance. See Art and Ritual and Science.
person/leonardo-da-vinci.observer: The Observer notes one individual who made pictures, studied anatomy and flight, and recorded it in mirror-writing that mostly stayed in notebooks. Because the notebooks were scattered after his death, his pattern-taming reached his contemporaries through paintings rather than publication, and only later did the notes show how far it went. His present fame also rests on status-signal: a price of $450 million for a disputed attribution measures a market as much as a picture.
questions: Is the Salvator Mundi by Leonardo, and how much of it?

person/li-qingzhao.title: Li Qingzhao
person/li-qingzhao.summary: Li Qingzhao (1084 to about 1155) was a Chinese poet of the Song dynasty, widely regarded as the greatest woman writer in the classical Chinese tradition. Her ci, a lyric verse form, moved from a settled, cultured life to loss and exile after northern China fell to invaders.
facts: She was born in 1084 in Qi Prefecture, today's Zhangqiu in Shandong, to a literary family, and is thought to have died about 1155.

In 1101 she married Zhao Mingcheng, a scholar who shared her interest in antiquities. The Jinshi lu, a catalog of bronze and stone inscriptions, is described as her husband's work and was published after his death.
When the Jin dynasty invaded northern China in 1127, the couple fled south with part of their collection, much of which is said to have been lost along the way. Zhao Mingcheng died in 1129.

After his death she wrote an afterword to the Jinshi lu describing their marriage and their losses. She briefly remarried, with the year traditionally given as about 1132, and divorced amid scandal soon after.

Her poems, mostly short ci in personal, direct language, describe love, separation, and later grief and displacement. Only around a hundred of her poems are known to survive, out of a larger body assembled and praised by later editors.
person/li-qingzhao.context: Li Qingzhao lived in East Asia during the Medieval Period, within the Song Dynasty, whose north fell to Jin invasion in 1127. See Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
person/li-qingzhao.observer: The Observer notes that her verse recorded an ordinary domestic partnership, book-collecting and companionship, that a state's collapse turned into flight and loss, and that this turn from ease to grief became the reason later readers kept her work in mark-code. A specialist could argue that only around a hundred surviving poems, out of a much larger and partly lost body, cannot support firm claims about how her style changed over her life, which would weaken any confident before-and-after reading.
questions: How much of her attributed work is authentic, given how much was lost after 1127?
What became of her after her brief second marriage?

person/liliuokalani.title: Liliuokalani
person/liliuokalani.summary: Liliuokalani (1838 to 1917) was the last monarch of the Kingdom of Hawaii, reigning from 1891 until she was deposed in January 1893 by a group of residents backed by United States troops.
facts: Liliuokalani was born in Honolulu on 2 September 1838 and died there on 11 November 1917.
She succeeded her brother Kalākaua on 29 January 1891 and was the kingdom's only reigning queen.
In January 1893 she moved to issue a constitution restoring royal powers reduced by the 1887 "Bayonet Constitution."

On 17 January 1893 a Committee of Safety of mostly American and European residents overthrew her while United States Marines were ashore. She yielded to the United States government to avoid bloodshed and asked it to reinstate her.
After a failed royalist uprising she was arrested and signed an abdication in January 1895.
Native Hawaiians submitted mass petitions against annexation in 1897, and the United States annexed Hawaii in 1898.
She composed songs, including "Aloha ʻOe," and published a memoir, Hawaii's Story by Hawaii's Queen, in 1898.
In 1993 the United States Congress apologized to Native Hawaiians for the overthrow, carried out with the participation of agents and citizens of the United States.
person/liliuokalani.context: Liliuokalani ruled a Native Hawaiian state in Oceania during the Industrial Age. Native Hawaiians descend from the Polynesians; see Polynesian Settlement of the Pacific. See Trade and Economy, Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
person/liliuokalani.observer: The Observer notes that Liliuokalani defended her kingdom's claim-line with the instruments her opponents also used: a written constitution, diplomatic appeals, and a published memoir. Her songs carried attachment to place and people in a form that outlasted the polity. The 1993 apology shows a claim-line redrawn by force being named as wrongful without being redrawn back. The reading of her as the main carrier of the resistance would weaken if the 1897 petitions show it rested chiefly on Native Hawaiian organizations.
questions: How much of the resistance to annexation came from Native Hawaiian organizations rather than from the queen?

person/louis-comfort-tiffany.title: Louis Comfort Tiffany
person/louis-comfort-tiffany.summary: Louis Comfort Tiffany (1848 to 1933) was an American designer whose iridescent Favrile glass, stained-glass windows and lamps became the signature look of American Art Nouveau. Recent scholarship credits many of his studio's best-known designs to staff designers, above all Clara Driscoll.
facts: Tiffany was born in New York in 1848, the son of the jeweller Charles Lewis Tiffany. He trained as a painter under George Inness before turning to interior design and decorative arts in the 1870s.

His firm redecorated state rooms in the White House in 1882 for President Chester Arthur; the work was later removed. In 1885 he founded what became Tiffany Studios, and in 1894 he trademarked the name Favrile.
His Byzantine-style chapel for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago won international acclaim. He built Laurelton Hall on Long Island as a showcase of his work.
Favrile glass builds iridescent, metallic colour into molten glass through mineral oxides. "Drapery glass" was manipulated while hot to form folds like fabric.
Financial losses, traced back to the 1920s and continuing into the Depression, forced the studio's closure. He died in New York in 1933.
Much of the detailed design of individual pieces, especially the lamps, was done by staff designers, above all Clara Driscoll, who led the women's glass-cutting department.

For most of the 20th century Tiffany was credited as sole designer. The mid-2000s rediscovery of Driscoll's letters credited her and the women of the "Tiffany Girls" department with several famous lamps, including the Dragonfly, a correction now generally accepted by museums and scholars.
person/louis-comfort-tiffany.context: Tiffany worked in North America in the Industrial Age. Christopher Dresser travelled to Japan in 1876 and 1877 partly on commission from Tiffany & Co., the jewellery firm founded by Tiffany's father. See Art and Ritual and Technology.
person/louis-comfort-tiffany.observer: The Observer notes that a name on the product credited one man for the work of a studio, and that the correction came from letters found a century later. The name worked as a brand, a status-signal that gathered credit upward, while the women who cut the glass and designed much of the work were recorded only in a side channel. The pattern of a maker's name absorbing a workshop is old. This case is unusually well documented because the letters survive.
questions: Which other famous Tiffany Studios pieces were designed by staff rather than by Tiffany?

person/ludwig-ii.title: Ludwig II
person/ludwig-ii.summary: Ludwig II (1845 to 1886), sometimes called the "Fairy Tale King," was King of Bavaria from 1864 until his death, remembered for building extravagant romantic castles and for his patronage of the composer Richard Wagner.
facts: He became an early and enthusiastic patron of Richard Wagner, paying off the composer's debts and funding productions, though political opposition to Wagner's influence at court eventually forced the composer to leave Munich.

He commissioned several elaborate castles, most famously Neuschwanstein, begun in 1869 and inspired partly by Wagner's operas; the castles were funded from his personal fortune rather than the Bavarian state treasury but still left him deeply in debt.

Bavaria's defeat alongside Austria in the 1866 Austro-Prussian War, and its incorporation into the German Empire in 1871, steadily reduced his practical political authority even as he retained the throne.

In 1886 a government commission, citing his mounting debts and reclusive behavior, had him declared mentally unfit to rule; he died under unclear circumstances in Lake Starnberg the day after being confined, an event still debated as accident, suicide, or possible foul play.
person/ludwig-ii.context: Ludwig II ruled Bavaria in Europe during the Industrial Age, overshadowed by Prussia's rise and German unification. See Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
person/ludwig-ii.observer: The Observer notes that Ludwig's declaration of mental incapacity came from a government that had strong political and financial reasons to remove him, and no independent medical examination confirmed the diagnosis before his death; the castles that nearly bankrupted him now draw more tourist revenue to Bavaria each year than they ever cost to build.
questions: Was Ludwig II's 1886 removal a legitimate response to incapacity, or a political maneuver by ministers and relatives seeking control of Bavaria's government?
