person/ramesses-ii.title: Ramesses II
person/ramesses-ii.summary: Ramesses II (about 1303 to 1213 BCE), also called Ramesses the Great, was the third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty. He ruled for about 66 years, fought the Hittites at Kadesh, made one of the earliest surviving peace treaties, and built temples across Egypt and Nubia.
facts: Ramesses II came to the throne in 1279 BCE by the most widely used chronology and reigned until 1213 BCE. Other chronologies differ by several years.

About 1274 BCE he fought the Hittite king Muwatalli II at Kadesh, in present-day Syria. Both sides claimed victory. Ramesses had it carved on temple walls, though most historians think the Hittites gained more.
About 1259 BCE he made a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III. It survives in Egyptian and Hittite versions, each saying the other side asked for peace first.
He built the capital Pi-Ramesses, the Ramesseum and the temples at Abu Simbel, moved in the 1960s to escape the Aswan High Dam reservoir. Many monuments carry his name over those of earlier kings.
He is estimated to have had more than 90 children and to have lived to about 90. His thirteenth son, Merneptah, succeeded him.
Later tradition links him to the pharaoh of the Exodus. Scholars dispute this, and no Egyptian source records such an event.
person/ramesses-ii.context: Ramesses II ruled in the Nile Valley in the Bronze Age. See Battle of Kadesh, Hittites, Ancient Egyptians and War and Conflict.
person/ramesses-ii.observer: The Observer notes that a battle with no clear winner was carved on several temples as a triumph, while the treaty that ended the rivalry survives in two versions that each say the other side asked first. Building on a huge scale, and carving his name over predecessors', worked as status-signal and story-glue. A specialist could argue that royal inscriptions followed conventions expected of any pharaoh, which would weaken a reading of monumentality as personal ambition.
questions: How did Kadesh look from the Hittite side, given that most Hittite records are fragmentary?
Which monuments bearing his name did he build, and which did he rework?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Ramesses II was the third pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty, acceding on 31 May 1279 BCE and dying on 13 August 1213 BCE after a reign of 66 years and 74 days [Wikipedia on Ramesses II]
2026-09-27: Ramesses II was born about 1303 BCE, and 90 or 91 is considered the most likely estimate of his age at death, though estimates vary [Wikipedia on Ramesses II]

2026-09-27: The Battle of Kadesh against the Hittite king Muwatalli II took place in his fifth regnal year (1274 BCE) and is generally considered a stalemate, though the Hittites were arguably the ultimate victors of the campaign because the Egyptians retreated afterwards [Wikipedia on Ramesses II]

2026-09-27: In his 21st regnal year (1259 BCE) Ramesses II concluded a treaty with the Hittite king Hattusili III, preserved in Egyptian hieroglyphic and Hittite cuneiform versions, each of which says the other side came suing for peace [Wikipedia on Ramesses II]
2026-09-27: Merneptah, who succeeded Ramesses II in 1213 BCE, was his thirteenth son and came to power only because his older brothers had died [Wikipedia on Merneptah]

person/rani-lakshmibai.title: Rani Lakshmibai
person/rani-lakshmibai.summary: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi (about 1828 to 1858) was an Indian queen who became a leader of the 1857 rebellion and a national symbol of resistance.
facts: She ruled Jhansi as regent after her husband's death, and the British refused to recognize her adopted heir.
She led the defense of Jhansi against British forces in 1858.
She and other rebels seized the fortress of Gwalior on 1 June 1858.
She died in battle on 17 June 1858.
person/rani-lakshmibai.context: She is a central figure of the Indian Rebellion of 1857 in South Asia.
person/rani-lakshmibai.observer: The Observer notes how a person killed in a lost war became a founding figure in a later nation's story. Defeat can be a source of legitimacy for the future.
questions: What were her actual aims in 1857?
fact_checks: 2026-09-20: Captured Gwalior 1 June 1858; died 17 June 1858 [National Army Museum on the Indian Rebellion; English Wikipedia]

person/razia-sultana.title: Razia Sultana
person/razia-sultana.summary: Razia Sultana (about 1205 to 1240) ruled the Delhi Sultanate from 1236 to 1240, the only woman to hold the throne in its history. She was the daughter of Iltutmish, who by tradition had named her his successor.
facts: Razia was a daughter of the sultan Iltutmish, who reigned from 1211 to 1236. Tradition holds that he named her his heir over his sons, though he seems to have chosen Ruknuddin Firuz shortly before his death.
After Iltutmish died in 1236 her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz took the throne but was deposed within months, and Razia became sultan with the support of the people of Delhi and some nobles.
According to chroniclers she held court in public and led armies; coins were issued in her name.
She appointed Jamal ud-Din Yaqut, an Abyssinian former slave, master of the stables, a promotion Turkic nobles resented.

In 1240 Malik Altunia, the governor of Bhatinda, rebelled. She was imprisoned at Bhatinda and then married him in September 1240; they were defeated at Kaithal and killed in October 1240, and accounts differ on the details.
The main contemporary account is by the chronicler Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani, who praised her abilities but wrote that her sex counted against her.
person/razia-sultana.context: Razia ruled the Delhi Sultanate in South Asia during the Medieval Period. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/razia-sultana.observer: The Observer notes that the complaints recorded against Razia concern who held high posts and who displayed the status-signals of rule, more than how she governed. Her only detailed account comes from a court chronicler who admired her and still described her sex as a defect. A specialist could argue that court histories overstated gender as the cause, since a quarrel between nobles and a strong sultan would look the same in the record.
questions: How much of the opposition to her was about her sex, and how much about court factions?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Razia was born about 1205 and died in October 1240 aged 34 to 35, with the date given as 15 October 1240 in the infobox but 13 October in the body text, so the exact day is uncertain [Wikipedia on Razia Sultan]

2026-09-27: Razia took the throne on 19 November 1236 after her half-brother Ruknuddin Firuz had reigned for less than seven months, with several nobles and the army pledging allegiance after a mob attacked the royal palace [Wikipedia on Razia Sultan]

2026-09-27: Razia appointed Malik Jamaluddin Yaqut, an Abyssinian, as Amir-i Akhur (master of the stables), a post previously held by Turkic officers, which created resentment among the Turkic nobles [Wikipedia on Razia Sultan]

2026-09-27: Iltutmish reigned from June 1211 to 30 April 1236 and is said to have declared Razia his heir apparent in 1231 after she administered Delhi during his Gwalior campaign, though he seems to have chosen Ruknuddin Firuz shortly before his death [Wikipedia on Iltutmish]

2026-09-27: Altunia of Tabarhinda (Bhatinda) rebelled in 1240 and Razia was imprisoned there, after which she married him in September 1240; they were defeated at Kaithal and killed in October 1240, more likely by their captors than by bandits as one later source says [Wikipedia on Razia Sultan]

person/rembrandt-van-rijn.title: Rembrandt van Rijn
person/rembrandt-van-rijn.summary: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn (15 July 1606 to 4 October 1669) was the greatest artist of the Dutch Golden Age, a painter, etcher and draughtsman. His roughly 100 self-portraits form an extraordinary autobiography, from early fame and wealth to bankruptcy and loss.
facts: Rembrandt was born in Leiden, the ninth child of a prosperous miller. He trained locally and for six months in Amsterdam with Pieter Lastman. About 1631 he moved to Amsterdam.

The Anatomy Lesson of Dr Nicolaes Tulp (1632) came early in his successful career as a portraitist in the city. In 1634 he married Saskia van Uylenburgh. Three of their children died in infancy; only Titus, born 1641, survived. Saskia died in 1642, the year he completed The Night Watch.
Debts led to bankruptcy in 1656, and his house and collection were sold. He kept working. His partner Hendrickje Stoffels died in 1663 and Titus in 1668.
He died on 4 October 1669 and was buried in a rented grave in the Westerkerk.
He used chiaroscuro to direct attention and mood. His late paintings are built from thick, rough layers applied with brush, palette knife and even fingers.
As a printmaker he combined etching with drypoint and varied each impression. Key works include The Hundred Guilder Print (about 1647 to 1649) and The Return of the Prodigal Son (about 1661 to 1669).
He ran a large workshop. Since 1968 the Rembrandt Research Project has reattributed many paintings. Goya is said to have named him one of his three masters.
person/rembrandt-van-rijn.context: Rembrandt worked in Europe during the Early Modern Period, in Amsterdam, then a booming commercial capital and home port of the Dutch East India Company. See Art and Ritual.
person/rembrandt-van-rijn.observer: The Observer notes a market of merchants, guilds and civic companies that paid for group portraits, while the same painter's late work found far fewer buyers, yet he kept working through bankruptcy and bereavement. The self-portraits are memory-outsourcing of a private face on a scale unusual for the age. Because he ran a large workshop, the line between his hand and his pupils' is a scholarly judgment that has moved since 1968, so the "Rembrandt" of any decade is partly a decision.
questions: Which paintings once credited to Rembrandt belong to his pupils, and which reattributions will hold?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn was born on 15 July 1606 in Leiden, the ninth child of Harmen Gerritszoon van Rijn, a miller [Wikipedia on Rembrandt]

2026-09-27: Rembrandt moved to Amsterdam at the end of 1631 and married Saskia van Uylenburgh in 1634; three of their children died within weeks of birth, only Titus (born 1641) survived to adulthood, and Saskia died in 1642, probably from tuberculosis [Wikipedia on Rembrandt]

2026-09-27: Hendrickje Stoffels died on 21 July 1663 and Titus van Rijn died on 4 September 1668, so Rembrandt outlived both [Wikipedia on Hendrickje Stoffels; Wikipedia on Titus van Rijn]

person/robert-the-bruce.title: Robert the Bruce
person/robert-the-bruce.summary: Robert the Bruce (1274 to 1329) was King of Scotland from 1306 to 1329, leading Scottish resistance to English rule and securing recognition of Scottish independence shortly before his death.
facts: He claimed the Scottish throne in 1306 after killing a rival claimant, John Comyn, in a church at Dumfries, an act that led to his excommunication by the pope.
Early in his reign he suffered several defeats and periods as a fugitive, including, according to a later popular legend, drawing perseverance from watching a spider repeatedly try to build its web.
He decisively defeated a much larger English army under Edward II at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314, the most significant Scottish military victory of the wars of independence.
The Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton in 1328 saw England formally recognize Scottish independence and Robert's kingship, a year before his death in 1329, reportedly from leprosy.
person/robert-the-bruce.context: Robert the Bruce led Scotland, in Europe, during the Medieval Period wars of independence against England. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/robert-the-bruce.observer: The Observer notes that Robert's path to the throne began with a killing in a church, not a conventional succession, and that his later reputation as Scotland's founding hero sits somewhat uneasily beside that origin; national founding stories often smooth over the more compromised beginnings of the figures they celebrate.
questions: How much of the spider legend and similar popular stories about Robert's perseverance date to his own lifetime versus later national mythmaking?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Robert the Bruce was born on 11 July 1274, probably at Turnberry Castle in Ayrshire, and died on 7 June 1329 at the Manor of Cardross in Dunbartonshire. [Wikipedia on Robert the Bruce]

2026-09-27: Robert killed John Comyn in the Greyfriars church at Dumfries on 10 February 1306 and was crowned at Scone on 25 March 1306, after which Pope Clement V excommunicated him. [Wikipedia on Robert the Bruce]

2026-09-27: The Scots under Robert the Bruce defeated Edward II at Bannockburn on 23-24 June 1314, against an English army estimated at 20,000 to 25,000 men versus 5,000 to 8,000 Scots, and the article calls it a decisive victory and a major turning point in the war. [Wikipedia on Battle of Bannockburn]

2026-09-27: The Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton was signed on 17 March 1328 and ratified at Northampton on 1 May 1328, with England recognising Scotland as independent and Robert the Bruce and his heirs as its rightful rulers. [Wikipedia on Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton]

2026-09-27: The cause of Robert's death is uncertain: some chroniclers mentioned leprosy, while modern scholars have proposed alternatives such as eczema, tuberculosis, motor neuron disease, cancer or strokes. [Wikipedia on Robert the Bruce]

person/rosalind-franklin.title: Rosalind Franklin
person/rosalind-franklin.summary: Rosalind Franklin (1920 to 1958) was a British chemist whose X-ray images of DNA were crucial to the discovery of its double-helix structure.
facts: 'Photo 51', an X-ray image of DNA, was taken in 1952 by Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling.
Her data were shown to James Watson without her knowledge and helped him and Francis Crick propose the structure in 1953.
She died of ovarian cancer at 37, four years before Watson, Crick, and Maurice Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize.
She also did important work on coal and on viruses.
person/rosalind-franklin.context: Franklin's work underlies the Genomic Revolution. Compare the career of Marie Curie.
person/rosalind-franklin.observer: The Observer notes that credit in science is itself a social system, and that it has not always been distributed fairly. The record of who found what depends on who told the story.
questions: How much credit did Franklin receive in her lifetime?

person/rumi.title: Rumi
person/rumi.summary: Rumi (Jalal ad-Din Muhammad Rumi, 1207 to 1273) was a Persian-language poet and Sufi teacher who spent his adult life in Konya, in Anatolia. His long poem, the Masnavi, and his lyric poems are among the most widely read works of Persian literature.
facts: Rumi was born in 1207 in Balkh or nearby Wakhsh, in present-day Afghanistan or Tajikistan; sources differ. His family moved west, and he was living in Konya, in the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, by about 1228.
He trained as a scholar and preacher like his father, Baha ad-Din Walad, and taught in Konya.

In 1244 he met a wandering mystic, Shams of Tabriz. Their friendship changed his life, and he began to write poetry. Shams disappeared about 1248, and accounts differ, with some saying he was killed and others that he simply moved on.
He wrote the Masnavi, a long poem in six books, and thousands of lyric poems collected in the Divan of Shams. He wrote mostly in Persian.

The Masnavi runs to some 25,000 to 27,000 couplets, with counts differing by source, composed over his last decade or so at the request of his disciple Husam al-Din Chalabi, who wrote the verses down as Rumi recited them. Some later readers called it "the Quran in Persian".
Fihi Ma Fihi ("In It What Is In It") is a prose collection of his informal talks to disciples, valued as the clearest record of how he taught.
He died in Konya on 17 December 1273. His followers founded the Mevlevi order, known for a ritual of whirling.
Loose English adaptations from the late 20th century onward made him, by some measures, one of the best-selling poets in the United States.
person/rumi.context: Rumi's family left the east in the years of the Mongol Conquests, and he lived in Levant and Anatolia during the Medieval Period. See Religion and Belief, Language and Writing and Art and Ritual.
person/rumi.observer: The Observer notes that a personal loss became the source of a body of verse that a community then turned into ritual, the whirling of the Mevlevi order, and a lineage. It shows one relationship carried across centuries by both sound-code and practice. A specialist could argue that later followers shaped the account of Shams and of Rumi's life, which would weaken any reading that treats the biography as settled.
questions: How much of the standard biography comes from accounts written by his followers after his death?

2026-09-27: Rumi died in Konya on 17 December 1273, and upon his death his followers and his son Sultan Walad founded the Mevlevi Order [Wikipedia on Rumi]
2026-09-27: The family finally settled in Konya on 1 May 1228, within the westernmost territories of the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum [Wikipedia on Rumi]
2026-09-27: Rumi met the dervish Shams-e Tabrizi on 15 November 1244, an encounter that completely changed his life [Wikipedia on Rumi]
2026-09-27: The Masnavi is a six-volume poem of approximately 27,000 lines, each a couplet with an internal rhyme, and has been commonly called 'the Quran in Persian' [Wikipedia on Rumi]

person/sacagawea.title: Sacagawea
person/sacagawea.summary: Sacagawea (about 1788 to 1812, or by another account 1884) was a young woman of disputed Shoshone or Hidatsa birth who traveled with the Lewis and Clark expedition from 1804 to 1806 as an interpreter, and later became one of the most commemorated women in the United States.
facts: Sacagawea was born about 1788, by tradition among the Lemhi Shoshone in present-day Idaho, though some recent work argues she was born Hidatsa.
About 1800 she was taken by a Hidatsa raiding party. As a teenager she married the trader Toussaint Charbonneau, and her son Jean Baptiste was born on 11 February 1805.

Charbonneau and Sacagawea joined the Lewis and Clark expedition at Fort Mandan in 1804. In August 1805 she met her brother Cameahwait, a Shoshone leader, whose horses the party needed to cross the Rockies.
Historians describe her chiefly as an interpreter and a sign of peaceful intent, more than a guide, though she gave directions in a few places.
A fur-trade clerk recorded in 1812 that Charbonneau's wife had died, but Shoshone oral tradition holds she lived until 1884 on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. Historians disagree.
Her name is spelled Sacagawea, Sacajawea and Sakakawea, the last from Hidatsa and used in North Dakota.
person/sacagawea.context: Sacagawea lived in North America on the eve of the westward expansion that led to events such as Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears. See Language and Writing and Trade and Economy.
person/sacagawea.observer: The Observer notes that a teenage mother with little say over her own life became one of the most commemorated women in the country, while the record was written almost entirely by the men she traveled with. Later suffragists made her story-glue for women's independence, a use she left no writing to confirm. A specialist could argue that neither her origin nor her death can be settled from the present documents, which would weaken any confident telling of her life.
questions: Was the woman who died in 1812 the same person as the woman buried in 1884?
What did she think of the journey, given no account in her own words survives?

person/saladin.title: Saladin
person/saladin.summary: Saladin (Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub, about 1137 to 1193) was a Kurdish-born Muslim commander who founded the Ayyubid dynasty, ruled Egypt and much of Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 1187.
facts: Saladin was born about 1137 in Tikrit, in present-day Iraq, to a Kurdish family, and died in Damascus on 4 March 1193.
He rose in the service of the Zengid ruler Nur ad-Din and became vizier of Fatimid Egypt in 1169.
In 1171 he ended the Fatimid Caliphate and restored Egypt's allegiance to the Abbasid caliph; his family, the Ayyubids, went on to rule Egypt and Syria.
After Nur ad-Din died in 1174 he took Damascus and brought much of Syria and northern Mesopotamia under his rule.

On 4 July 1187 his army destroyed a Crusader army at the Battle of Hattin. Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October 1187, and its Latin inhabitants could ransom themselves, though many who could not pay were enslaved.
In the Third Crusade he fought Richard I of England. The Treaty of Ramla (September 1192) left the Crusaders a coastal strip and allowed Christian pilgrims to visit Jerusalem.
person/saladin.context: Saladin's wars took place in Levant and Anatolia during the Medieval Period; see Crusades. See War and Conflict, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
person/saladin.observer: The Observer notes that Jerusalem, sacred to three traditions, was taken by force in 1099 and again in 1187, with very different treatment of the defeated, and that Saladin's reputation for restraint rests largely on his own court biographers and on Crusader writers who admired it. The war against the Crusaders also served as a story-glue that let him unite rival Muslim rulers under his command. A specialist could argue that the terms of 1187 reflect a negotiated surrender rather than his character, which would weaken the reading of restraint as a personal trait.
questions: How much of his reputation for restraint comes from his own court biographers?

person/sappho.title: Sappho
person/sappho.summary: Sappho (about 630 to about 570 BCE) was a Greek lyric poet from the island of Lesbos whose songs of love, longing and ritual were collected in at least eight books, possibly nine, in antiquity. Only fragments survive, plus one complete poem.
facts: Sappho was born about 630 BCE on Lesbos in the eastern Aegean, in Mytilene or Eresos according to ancient sources; her dates are approximate.
She composed songs in Aeolic Greek to be sung with a lyre, and the Sapphic stanza is named after her.
Ancient scholars gathered her poems in at least eight books, possibly nine. Only fragments survive, apart from one complete poem, a prayer to Aphrodite (Fragment 1).
New papyrus fragments published in 2004 and 2014 added lines, including a poem that mentions her brothers.
Many surviving poems express desire for women. Scholars debate whether her circle on Lesbos was a religious association, a school for girls, or a social group.
Ancient sources say she spent time in exile in Sicily and had a daughter, Cleis. The biography is largely unreliable.
The words "sapphic" and "lesbian" derive from her name and her island.
person/sappho.context: Sappho wrote in Greek, in the Alphabet, among the Ancient Greeks of the Mediterranean Basin during the Iron Age. See Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
person/sappho.observer: The Observer notes that Sappho was copied for centuries and then largely lost, so the poet known today is a set of quotations and scraps, some recovered on papyri from Egyptian sites. Most claims about her life come from writers who lived centuries later and read her poems as autobiography. Any portrait therefore reflects what survived and what later readers wanted from a story-glue about desire and grief. New papyri could change the picture, so the reading should be held loosely.
questions: What was the purpose of the circle of women around her?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Sappho is dated c. 630 to c. 570 BC, and the c. marks these as approximate dates [Wikipedia on Sappho]
2026-09-27: Sappho was an ancient Greek poet from Eresos or Mytilene on the island of Lesbos [Wikipedia on Sappho]
2026-09-27: Only the Ode to Aphrodite is certainly complete, and only about 650 of her roughly 10,000 lines survive [Wikipedia on Sappho]

person/savitribai-phule.title: Savitribai Phule
person/savitribai-phule.summary: Savitribai Phule (1831 to 1897) was an Indian educator, poet and social reformer in Maharashtra who, with her husband Jyotirao Phule, opened one of the first schools for girls in Pune in 1848. She died of plague in 1897 after nursing patients.
facts: Savitribai Phule was born on 3 January 1831 in Naigaon, Maharashtra, and married Jyotirao Phule in 1840 as a child. He taught her to read.

In 1848 the couple opened a school for girls in Pune. She is often called India's first woman teacher; earlier girls' schools existed, so the "first" claim is contested, and historians also credit Fatima Sheikh as a co-worker.
Accounts say she was harassed with stones and dung on her way to teach.
She and Jyotirao later opened further schools, including for children of lower castes, and in 1863 they founded a home for the prevention of infanticide.
She published a book of poetry, Kavya Phule, in 1854.
She died on 10 March 1897 in Pune after catching plague while nursing patients during an outbreak.
person/savitribai-phule.context: Savitribai Phule worked in South Asia under the British Raj in the Industrial Age, when schooling and caste were contested subjects. See Kinship and Society and Language and Writing.
person/savitribai-phule.observer: The Observer notes that in her setting, literacy in the mark-code was itself a marker of caste and gender privilege, and she moved it across those lines at real personal cost. Her poems survive as her own writing, unlike much of what is said about her, which comes from later admiring accounts. A specialist could argue that the popular "first female teacher" story hides other women who taught girls, which would weaken the reading that she acted alone.
questions: How much of the harassment story comes from contemporary sources and how much from later tradition?

person/seondeok.title: Seondeok
person/seondeok.summary: Queen Seondeok (birth year unknown, died 647 CE) ruled the Korean kingdom of Silla as its first reigning queen, a period marked by Buddhist temple building, early astronomical observation and continued warfare with the rival kingdoms of Baekje and Goguryeo.
facts: She succeeded her father, King Jinpyeong, in 632 after he left no surviving son, becoming Silla's first female monarch in her own right.

Her reign saw the construction of Cheomseongdae, often described as one of the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in East Asia, and the Hwangnyongsa nine-story pagoda, built to help protect the kingdom according to Buddhist belief.

Silla faced repeated attacks from Baekje during her reign, including the loss of border fortresses, and she decided to form a military alliance with Tang China, with her general Kim Yushin and diplomat Kim Chunchu, later King Muyeol, traditionally credited with the negotiations.
A rebellion by the noble Bidam against her rule broke out in 647 and was suppressed by Kim Yushin and Kim Alcheon shortly after her death that same year, which some accounts link to the unrest.
person/seondeok.context: Seondeok ruled in East Asia during the Medieval Period, and the Tang alliance her court pursued eventually enabled Silla's unification of most of the Korean peninsula after her reign. See Religion and Belief, Science and Kinship and Society.
person/seondeok.observer: The Observer notes that later chroniclers, writing under a dynasty uneasy about female rule, framed Seondeok's reign partly through omens and prophecy rather than policy, which can make her recorded wisdom look more like folklore than governance. The observatory and pagoda, built objects rather than reported speech, are harder to dismiss and point to a court capable of sustained, costly projects.
questions: How much of the surviving account of her reign reflects later Silla or Goryeo-era attitudes toward female sovereignty rather than contemporary record?

person/sequoyah.title: Sequoyah
person/sequoyah.summary: Sequoyah (about 1770 to 1843) was a Cherokee silversmith who created the Cherokee syllabary, a writing system for the Cherokee language, completed by 1821. It is one of the few writing systems whose invention by a single known person is well documented.
facts: Sequoyah was born about 1770 in the Cherokee town of Tuskegee, in present-day Tennessee; the birth year is approximate.
He did not read or write English. He began work on a writing system for Cherokee about 1809 and completed it by 1821.
The syllabary has 85 characters (86 in early versions), each standing for a syllable.
The system spread rapidly among the Cherokee. The Cherokee Phoenix, a newspaper printed in Cherokee and English, began publication in 1828 and was the first Native newspaper in the United States.
He later lived among Cherokee who had moved west of the Mississippi River. He died in August 1843 in Mexico while searching for a group of Cherokee said to have settled there.
person/sequoyah.context: Sequoyah's work belongs to the history of writing; see Invention of Writing. The Cherokee were among the nations forced west by Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears. He lived in North America in the Industrial Age. See Language and Writing and Technology.
person/sequoyah.observer: The Observer notes that a man who could not read any writing designed a mark-code for his own sound-code, and that according to the accounts a whole people took it up within a few years, a rare case where the inventor of a writing system is known. That it spread among a people under pressure on their land shows memory-outsourcing serving to hold a community together and to deal with a state that ran on paper. The reading would weaken if evidence showed he drew more on existing writing systems than the accounts suggest.
questions: How did he arrive at the syllable approach, and how much did he know of other writing systems?

2026-09-27: Sequoyah never went to school and never learned English, began creating a writing system for Cherokee around 1809, and completed his syllabary in 1821. [Wikipedia on Sequoyah]

2026-09-27: The syllabary was first made with 86 symbols, each a consonant-vowel sequence or syllable, and was later streamlined to 85 after the 86th character was dropped in 1828. [Wikipedia on Sequoyah; Wikipedia on Cherokee syllabary]

person/sergei-eisenstein.title: Sergei Eisenstein
person/sergei-eisenstein.summary: Sergei Eisenstein (1898 to 1948) was a Soviet film director and theorist, born in Riga, who argued that meaning came from the collision between shots rather than any single image. His Odessa Steps massacre sequence in Battleship Potemkin (1925) remains one of cinema's most studied passages.
facts: Eisenstein was born in Riga in 1898, son of an architect and civil engineer, and trained in engineering and architecture before turning to the arts.
The Russian Revolution pushed him into theatre; he joined Meyerhold's Proletkult Theatre before moving into film in the early 1920s.
His second feature, Battleship Potemkin (1925), made for the twentieth anniversary of the 1905 Revolution, brought him international fame.
In Strike (1925) he pioneered "intellectual montage," cutting colliding images together and favoring crowds and non-professional "types" over trained stars.
Invited to Hollywood then Mexico in the early 1930s, both projects went unfinished, and his 1937 Soviet film Bezhin Meadow was suppressed and reportedly destroyed.
He regained official favor with Alexander Nevsky (1938), scored by Sergei Prokofiev, extending his editing style to sound and mass combat.

He spent his final years on Ivan the Terrible; Part I won a Stalin Prize, but Part II, completed in 1946, was criticized by various authorities and went unreleased until 1958; Eisenstein died of a heart attack in Moscow in 1948.
His writings, including Film Form and The Film Sense, became foundational film-studies texts, and he is ranked among cinema's most important directors and theorists.
person/sergei-eisenstein.context: Eisenstein worked in the Soviet Union, within Europe, during the Industrial Age; the Russian Revolution redirected him from engineering into theatre and film, and his breakthrough film commemorated the revolutionary struggle before it. His staged battles and massacres connect him to War and Conflict and Art and Ritual.
person/sergei-eisenstein.observer: The Observer finds a subject who treated the edit itself as an argument: meaning, he held, was made not inside a single image but in the collision between two, an engineered story-glue built into a film's machinery. His preference for crowds and "type"-cast non-professionals over trained performers made the collective, not the individual, the vehicle for a revolutionary meaning-engine. The staged violence recurring through his films, a factory massacre, a staircase shooting, a battle on ice, reads as a fascination with sanctioned harm as spectacle. That the same state whose myths he helped build also suppressed one film and held back another shows how uneasily a master of persuasion sat within the system he served.
questions: Since the negative of Bezhin Meadow (1937) is reported to have been destroyed after its suppression, what the finished film actually contained is now unknown.

person/sesshu-toyo.title: Sesshū Tōyō
person/sesshu-toyo.summary: Sesshū Tōyō (1420 to 1506) was a Japanese Zen monk and painter who studied Chinese ink painting in Ming China and made it a Japanese art. He is regarded as the greatest master of Japanese ink painting.
facts: Sesshū was born in 1420 in Bitchū Province (present-day Okayama Prefecture) and entered a Zen temple as a boy. He studied painting at Shōkoku-ji in Kyoto with the monk-painter Tenshō Shūbun.
About the 1460s he took the name Sesshū ("snow boat") and settled in Yamaguchi under the patronage of the Ōuchi family.
In 1467 he joined a trade mission to Ming China and spent about two to three years there (sources differ), travelling to Beijing and receiving an honorary title at the Tiantong monastery near Ningbo.

He returned to Japan about 1469, as the Ōnin War was tearing Kyoto apart, and worked in the provinces from his studio, the Unkoku-an, in Yamaguchi. He is credited with designing several temple gardens and died in 1506.

He painted in suibokuga, black ink and water on paper or silk, including the loose haboku ("broken ink") manner. Key works include Haboku Landscape (1495), Huike Offering His Arm to Bodhidharma (1496) and View of Ama-no-Hashidate (about 1501 to 1506).
Six of his works are designated National Treasures of Japan, more than any other painter.
The Unkoku school continued his studio, and Hasegawa Tōhaku styled himself Sesshū's fifth-generation heir. In 1956 the World Peace Council named him one of its "great cultural figures".
person/sesshu-toyo.context: Sesshū's travel to the Ming Dynasty linked his work to East Asia beyond Japan during the Medieval Period. See Art and Ritual and Religion and Belief.
person/sesshu-toyo.observer: The Observer notes a tool-lineage of brush and ink that crossed the sea as a Chinese import in Zen monasteries and became a Japanese possession, carried by a monk on a trade mission, an exchange-web moving skill as well as goods. Later schools claiming descent from him, and a painter who styled himself fifth-generation heir, show ancestor-weight running the other way: a lineage can be asserted after the fact. Which of the works attributed to him are his own is not settled.
questions: Which of the works attributed to Sesshū are by his own hand?

person/shaka.title: Shaka
person/shaka.summary: Shaka kaSenzangakhona (about 1787 to 1828) was the founder of the Zulu Kingdom, who transformed its military and political organization.
facts: He came to power around 1816 and expanded the Zulu state quickly.
He is credited with new weapons and tactics, including the short stabbing spear and a 'buffalo horns' formation.
He was assassinated in 1828 by his half-brothers.
Much of what is told about him comes from colonial-era European accounts and oral tradition, and is debated.
person/shaka.context: See Zulu Kingdom and Mfecane.
person/shaka.observer: The Observer notes that Shaka's image has been shaped by colonial writers who found it convenient to portray him as a tyrant. See Who Writes the Record.
questions: How reliable are the early accounts of Shaka?

person/shen-zhou.title: Shen Zhou
person/shen-zhou.summary: Shen Zhou (1427 to 1509) was a scholar-painter of Ming-dynasty China who founded the Wu School in Suzhou. He never held office, and his landscapes combine painting, poetry and calligraphy as a record of friendship and quiet life.
facts: Shen Zhou was born in 1427 near Suzhou in the Jiangnan region, into a wealthy family of scholars, poets and collectors. His grandfather and father were painters, and the family avoided government service.
He never sat the civil service examinations. When local officials recommended him for office he declined, saying he had to care for his widowed mother, who lived to almost 100.
His home became a meeting place for Suzhou's intellectual elite, and many paintings were made as gifts for friends, marking birthdays, farewells or shared outings.
He painted "in the manner of" the four great Yuan masters, Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen, Ni Zan and Wang Meng. Almost every painting carries his own poem in his calligraphy.
He was one of the first Chinese painters to make albums of real local places around Suzhou. Key works include Lofty Mount Lu (1467), Night Vigil (1492) and Poet on a Mountaintop (about 1500).
Through his pupil Wen Zhengming the Wu School dominated Chinese painting in the 16th century. With Wen Zhengming, Tang Yin and Qiu Ying he is counted among the "Four Masters of the Ming Dynasty".
According to one story, when forgers sold fake Shen Zhou paintings, he sometimes signed them to help them earn a living. He died in 1509, aged 82.
Later theorists such as Dong Qichang placed him in the "Southern School" of literati painters, whom they judged superior to professional court artists.
person/shen-zhou.context: Shen Zhou lived under the Ming Dynasty in East Asia during the Medieval Period. See Art and Ritual.
person/shen-zhou.observer: The Observer notes a painter who refused office and made pictures for friends, so that art served as a currency of obligation and affection rather than of sale. His habit of painting in the manner of older masters treats the past as a conversation, an explicit form of ancestor-weight. The later ranking of scholar-painters above court artists came from theorists such as Dong Qichang, so the hierarchy is itself a later judgement, and the anecdotes of his generosity are the kind that gather around admired figures.
questions: How many surviving works attributed to Shen Zhou are authentic, given that forgeries circulated in his lifetime?

person/siddhartha-gautama.title: Siddhartha Gautama
person/siddhartha-gautama.summary: Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, was a spiritual teacher in northern India whose teachings founded Buddhism. Traditional dates are about 563 to 483 BCE, but modern scholarship suggests a somewhat later range.
facts: Buddhist tradition holds that he left a princely life and attained awakening at Bodh Gaya.
His teachings include the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path.
The exact dates of his life are debated among scholars.
Buddhism later spread across Asia via monks and trade routes.
person/siddhartha-gautama.context: He is a central figure of the Axial Age in South Asia. The emperor Ashoka later promoted Buddhism widely.
person/siddhartha-gautama.observer: The Observer notes that a movement that rejected the idea of a permanent self attracted millions of followers over centuries. The tradition treats craving as the root of suffering, an analysis that has parallels in modern psychology.

person/simon-bolivar.title: Simón Bolívar
person/simon-bolivar.summary: Simón Bolívar (1783 to 1830) was a Venezuelan military and political leader who led the independence of several South American countries from Spain and tried to unite them as Gran Colombia.
facts: He was born in Caracas to a wealthy family.
He and Sucre led the campaigns that freed present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia.
He met José de San Martín at Guayaquil in 1822.
Gran Colombia split apart within seven years, and Bolívar died in 1830.
person/simon-bolivar.context: Bolívar is the central figure of the Latin American Wars of Independence, part of the Age of Revolutions.
person/simon-bolivar.observer: The Observer notes that a leader who liberated half a continent died convinced that his project had failed. Success in founding states does not guarantee holding them together.
questions: Why did Gran Colombia break apart?

person/sitting-bull.title: Sitting Bull
person/sitting-bull.summary: Sitting Bull (Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake, born between 1831 and 1837, died 1890) was a Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man who resisted United States expansion onto Lakota lands and was in the camp at the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876. Native police killed him in 1890.
facts: Sitting Bull was born sometime between 1831 and 1837, traditionally on the Grand River in present-day South Dakota (a 2007 family oral tradition places his birth on the Yellowstone River instead), and became a leading Hunkpapa Lakota war leader and holy man.
The Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) guaranteed the Black Hills to the Lakota. After gold was found there in 1874 the United States sought to take the land, and war followed in 1876.

On 25 and 26 June 1876 Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors destroyed the force of Lt. Col. George Custer at the Little Bighorn. Sitting Bull was in the large camp; accounts describe his role as spiritual leader and organizer rather than field commander.
After the battle he led his followers to Canada in 1877, and he surrendered at Fort Buford in July 1881.
On 15 December 1890, at Standing Rock, Native police sent to arrest him amid tension over the Ghost Dance killed him in a struggle. The Wounded Knee massacre followed on 29 December.
person/sitting-bull.context: Sitting Bull's Lakota faced the same expansion of the United States that drove earlier removals of eastern nations; see Indian Removal and the Trail of Tears. He lived in North America during the Industrial Age. See War and Conflict, Religion and Belief and Kinship and Society.
person/sitting-bull.observer: The Observer notes that Sitting Bull is remembered as a war leader though the accounts place him as a spiritual leader at the Little Bighorn, a case of the record following the battle's fame rather than the man's role. His killing by Native police employed by the agency he opposed shows how a state can turn a community's own members into instruments of its claim-line. The reading would weaken if fuller Lakota accounts gave him a more central military role.
questions: What do Lakota oral accounts say about his role at the Little Bighorn?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Sitting Bull was a Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man born on land later included in the Dakota Territory (the Grand River is the listed birthplace), sometime between 1831 and 1837, so the year is uncertain; a 2007 family oral tradition instead places his birth on the Yellowstone River [Wikipedia on Sitting Bull]

2026-09-27: At the Little Bighorn Sitting Bull did not act as a field commander but as a spiritual leader, after a Sun Dance vision in which he foresaw soldiers falling into his camp [Wikipedia on Sitting Bull; Wikipedia on Battle of the Little Bighorn]

2026-09-27: The Battle of the Little Bighorn was fought on 25 and 26 June 1876 by Lakota, Northern Cheyenne and Arapaho forces against the 7th Cavalry under Lt. Col. George Custer, whose battalion was destroyed and who was killed [Wikipedia on Battle of the Little Bighorn]
2026-09-27: Sitting Bull led his band north to Wood Mountain in Canada in May 1877 and surrendered at Fort Buford on 19 July 1881 [Wikipedia on Sitting Bull]

2026-09-27: Sitting Bull was shot dead on 15 December 1890 at Standing Rock during an attempted arrest by Indian police officers, amid fear that he would join the Ghost Dance movement [Wikipedia on Sitting Bull]

person/sofonisba-anguissola.title: Sofonisba Anguissola
person/sofonisba-anguissola.summary: Sofonisba Anguissola (about 1532 to 1629) was an Italian portrait painter from Cremona, one of the first women in Europe to build a professional career as a painter. She spent years at the Spanish court, traditionally put at about 14, and won international fame.
facts: Sofonisba was born about 1532 in Cremona, the eldest of seven children of Amilcare Anguissola, a minor nobleman. He gave all his daughters a humanist education, and several became painters. She studied with Bernardino Campi and Bernardino Gatti.
As a noblewoman she could not study anatomy from the nude or take large public commissions, so she made portraiture her field.
Her father sent her drawings to Michelangelo, who reportedly challenged her to draw a crying boy. She answered with Boy Bitten by a Crayfish, a drawing that circulated widely.

In 1559 she was invited to Madrid to serve Queen Elisabeth of Valois, wife of Philip II, as lady-in-waiting and painting teacher. She painted the royal court for a period traditionally given as about 14 years, though sources differ, and the Spanish court arranged her marriage to a Sicilian nobleman, Fabrizio de Moncada.

After his death she married a Genoese sea captain and lived in Genoa and Palermo. In 1629 Anthony van Dyck visited her in Palermo (an earlier reading gave 1624) and recorded her advice. She died there in 1629 (older sources say 1625), in her mid-to-late nineties.
Key works include The Chess Game (1555), Self-Portrait at the Easel (about 1556) and Portrait of Philip II of Spain (1565).
Many of her court works were later credited to male painters such as Sánchez Coello, and scholars have restored many to her name. The Prado's 2019 exhibition paired her with Lavinia Fontana.
person/sofonisba-anguissola.context: Sofonisba worked in Europe during the Renaissance and the Early Modern Period. Michelangelo encouraged her, and her success opened the way for later women painters such as Artemisia Gentileschi. Some scholars link her Boy Bitten by a Crayfish to Caravaggio's Boy Bitten by a Lizard. See Art and Ritual and Kinship and Society.
person/sofonisba-anguissola.observer: The Observer notes that the limits placed on her, no study from the nude and no large public commissions, shaped the genre she made her own, so that a social rule produced a new kind of picture. Her career also depended on a father who promoted her and a court that hired her, a case of the kin-lattice acting as an agency. That many court works were credited to male painters shows how attribution follows expectation. Restoring them is a correction that is still under way.
questions: Which court portraits now credited to other painters are by Anguissola?

person/sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz.title: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
person/sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz.summary: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (born 1648 or 1651, died 1695) was a nun, poet and playwright in colonial Mexico City. She is regarded as one of the leading Spanish-language writers of the seventeenth century and an early defender of women's right to study.
facts: Juana Ramírez de Asbaje was born at San Miguel Nepantla, near Mexico City. Baptismal records point to 1648 or 1651, and the year is debated. She died on 17 April 1695.
Largely self-taught, she served at the viceroy's court in her teens and in 1669 entered the Hieronymite convent of San Jerónimo.
She wrote lyric poems, plays such as Los empeños de una casa (1683) and the long poem Primero sueño. Her first collection, Inundación castálida, was printed in Madrid in 1689.

In 1690 the Bishop of Puebla published her critique of a sermon by António Vieira as the Carta atenagórica and, writing as "Sor Filotea," urged her toward religious study. She answered in 1691 with the Respuesta a Sor Filotea de la Cruz, defending women's right to learn.
In 1693 and 1694 she stopped writing and signed penitential documents. Whether she sold her library or had it taken, and how far the choice was hers, is debated.
She died in the plague of 1695 while nursing other sisters.
person/sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz.context: Sor Juana lived in Mesoamerica during the Early Modern Period, in a Mexico City built over Tenochtitlan and ruled by Spain after the Spanish Conquest of the Aztec Empire. See Art and Ritual and Language and Writing.
person/sor-juana-ines-de-la-cruz.observer: The Observer notes that the convent gave her a room, books and time at the price of vows. The meaning-engine that sheltered her writing later restrained it. A specialist could argue that the silence of 1693 was her own choice, or that the surviving documents are formulaic, which would weaken a reading of her as simply silenced.
questions: Was her final silence chosen, forced, or both?
Which accounts of her library's fate rest on documents?

2026-09-27: She briefly entered a Discalced Carmelite monastery in 1667 and in 1669 entered the Hieronymite convent, taking the name Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz [Wikipedia on Juana Inés de la Cruz]
2026-09-27: Her collection Inundación castálida was published in Madrid in 1689, and her play Los empeños de una casa was first performed on 4 October 1683 [Wikipedia on Juana Inés de la Cruz]

person/sukarno.title: Sukarno
person/sukarno.summary: Sukarno (1901 to 1970) was the leader of Indonesia's independence movement and its first president. He proclaimed independence in 1945, ruled until 1967, and was removed from power after the killings of 1965 and 1966.
facts: Sukarno was born on 6 June 1901 in Surabaya, in the Dutch East Indies, and died on 21 June 1970 in Jakarta, under house arrest.
He founded the Indonesian National Party in 1927. The Dutch arrested him in 1929 and released him in 1931, then exiled him to Flores in 1934 and to Sumatra in 1938.

He cooperated with the Japanese occupation from 1942 to 1945, which forced millions into labor and whose food requisitions contributed to a famine that killed over a million people in Java in 1944 and 1945.
On 1 June 1945 he presented Pancasila, five founding principles for the state, and on 17 August 1945 he proclaimed independence, becoming president the next day.
He hosted the Bandung Conference of Asian and African states in 1955 and introduced "Guided Democracy" in 1959, ending parliamentary rule.

After the 30 September Movement of 1965, an army-led campaign killed between 500,000 and over a million people, mostly communists and alleged sympathizers. General Suharto took power in 1966 and 1967.
person/sukarno.context: Sukarno worked in Southeast Asia during the Information Age, in the years of Decolonization and the Cold War. See War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
person/sukarno.observer: The Observer notes that a nation spread over thousands of islands was named and given five founding principles before its state existed, story-glue in its plainest form. He tried to hold nationalist, religious and communist camps under one roof, and the arrangement broke in 1965 in mass killing. A specialist could argue that army and foreign pressures made the collapse of Guided Democracy likely whatever he chose, which would weaken a reading that places the outcome in his leadership.
questions: What role did he play, if any, in the events of 30 September 1965?
How much did his wartime cooperation with Japan cost, and how much did it gain?

2026-09-27: Sukarno delivered the Pancasila speech on 1 June 1945, proclaimed Indonesian independence on 17 August 1945, and was elected president by the PPKI on 18 August [Wikipedia on Sukarno]

person/suleiman-the-magnificent.title: Suleiman the Magnificent
person/suleiman-the-magnificent.summary: Suleiman the Magnificent (1494 to 1566) was Ottoman sultan from 1520 to 1566, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent, military power, and legal and cultural achievement.
facts: His armies captured Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522, then advanced deep into Central Europe, defeating and killing the King of Hungary at the Battle of Mohacs in 1526, though a first siege of Vienna in 1529 failed to take the city.

Known by the epithet Kanuni (the Lawgiver), which is absent from sixteenth and seventeenth-century Ottoman sources and may date only from the early 18th century, he issued a major legal code harmonizing Ottoman civil law with Islamic religious law across the empire's diverse territories.

His navies under admirals such as Barbarossa Hayreddin Pasha contested Mediterranean control with Spain and its allies, and Ottoman forces also pushed into Persia and Mesopotamia, capturing Baghdad in 1534.
His reign saw a major flourishing of Ottoman architecture under the chief architect Mimar Sinan, and of court poetry, painting, and decorative arts, centered on Istanbul.
person/suleiman-the-magnificent.context: Suleiman led the Ottoman Empire from Levant and Anatolia during the Early Modern Period, extending its reach across three continents. See War and Conflict, Religion and Belief and Trade and Economy.
person/suleiman-the-magnificent.observer: The Observer notes that Suleiman's failed 1529 siege of Vienna, rather than his many successes, marked the practical limit of Ottoman expansion into Central Europe for the rest of his reign; the empire's reputation for irresistible advance rested on decades of victories that stopped, in the end, at a single unsuccessful siege.
questions: How much did overextended supply lines, rather than Habsburg defense alone, determine the failure of the 1529 siege of Vienna?

2026-09-27: Ottoman forces took Belgrade in 1521 and Rhodes in 1522 after a five-month siege, and on 29 August 1526 Suleiman defeated Louis II of Hungary at Mohacs, where the king and much of the Hungarian aristocracy were killed [Wikipedia on Suleiman the Magnificent]

person/sun-tzu.title: Sun Tzu
person/sun-tzu.summary: Sun Tzu (traditionally about 544 to 496 BCE) is the name attached to The Art of War, the most influential text on military strategy from ancient China, said to have served the state of Wu. Whether he was one historical person is disputed.
facts: Tradition places Sun Tzu, personal name Sun Wu, as a general who advised King Helü of Wu in the late 6th century BCE. The Art of War is organized in about 13 short chapters.
The historian Sima Qian, writing centuries later, told a story of Sun Tzu proving his discipline by drilling the king's concubines, executing two who disobeyed. Scholars treat this as legend.
His name appears in no text earlier than Sima Qian's history, and one theory holds "Sun Wu" was a made-up title, with the Art of War actually the work of his supposed descendant Sun Bin.

In 1972 bamboo strips from a Han tomb at Yinqueshan included versions of both the Art of War and a separate text by Sun Bin, confirming the Art of War circulated early and that Sun Bin was a distinct author.
The text has shaped military and business thought for over two thousand years, and is translated worldwide.
person/sun-tzu.context: Sun Tzu's traditional dates place him in East Asia near the end of the Iron Age, roughly contemporary with Confucius. See War and Conflict and Language and Writing.
person/sun-tzu.observer: The Observer notes that a text on organized, calculated sanctioned harm has outlived any certainty about who wrote it, carried forward in mark-code through copies made centuries after the events it claims. The 1972 tomb find settled that the text existed early, without settling who composed it. A specialist could argue "Sun Tzu" was a legendary attribution rather than a single author, which would weaken any biographical reading of the text's origin.
questions: Was Sun Tzu a real individual, a legendary figure, or a name attached to a composite text?
How much of the Art of War as read today reflects its earliest version found at Yinqueshan?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Sun Tzu, birth name Sun Wu, is traditionally dated to 544 to 496 BCE and is said to have been a minister to King Helü of Wu [Wikipedia on Sun Tzu]

2026-09-27: The earliest account of Sun Tzu's life is in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (around 97 BCE), which tells how he had two of the king's concubines executed when they disobeyed his drill orders [Wikipedia on Sun Tzu]

2026-09-27: The name Sun Wu does not appear in any text before the Records of the Grand Historian, the Zuo Zhuan does not mention Sun Tzu at all, and from about the 12th century Chinese scholars began to doubt his historical existence [Wikipedia on Sun Tzu; Wikipedia on The Art of War]

2026-09-27: Bamboo slips found at Yinqueshan in 1972 and sealed between 134 and 118 BCE held two separate texts, one matching the received Art of War and another attributed to Sun Bin [Wikipedia on Sun Tzu; Wikipedia on The Art of War]
2026-09-27: The Art of War is composed of 13 chapters, each devoted to a different set of skills related to warfare [Wikipedia on The Art of War]

person/sun-yat-sen.title: Sun Yat-sen
person/sun-yat-sen.summary: Sun Yat-sen (1866 to 1925) was a Chinese revolutionary and physician who worked for decades to overthrow the Qing dynasty and became the first provisional president of the Republic of China in 1912. Both mainland China and Taiwan honor him as a founder.
facts: Sun Yat-sen was born on 12 November 1866 in Cuiheng, Guangdong, and died on 12 March 1925 in Beijing. He was educated in Hawaii and trained as a doctor in Hong Kong, graduating in 1892.
He founded the Revive China Society in 1894, after an earlier reform petition was rejected, and organized several failed uprisings against the Qing from 1895 onward.
In Tokyo in 1905 he founded the Tongmenghui, which grew to about a thousand members, and set out his Three Principles of the People: nationalism, democracy and people's livelihood.

The Wuchang uprising of 10 October 1911, which he did not lead in person, began the revolution that ended the Qing dynasty. He returned from abroad and served as provisional president from 1 January 1912, resigning that March to Yuan Shikai.
He rebuilt his Kuomintang party in 1919, and in 1923 allied it with the Soviet Union and the small Chinese Communist Party.
In 1904 he obtained a certificate claiming birth in Hawaii in 1870, later renounced; his standard birth year and place are not in doubt.
person/sun-yat-sen.context: Sun Yat-sen worked in East Asia during the Industrial Age, and the Xinhai Revolution of 1911 that he had long prepared for ended the Qing Dynasty. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/sun-yat-sen.observer: The Observer notes that decades of failed uprisings built a network and an ideology, story-glue in the Three Principles, that outlasted any single attempt at sanctioned harm. He was abroad when the revolution he had long prepared for finally succeeded, and held power only briefly before yielding it. A specialist could argue his greatest effect was organizational and rhetorical rather than military, which would weaken a reading that credits him with the 1911 victory itself.
questions: How much did his organizing directly cause the 1911 uprising, given he was not present for it?
What did his 1923 alliance with the Soviet Union and the Communists commit his party to?

person/sundiata-keita.summary: Sundiata Keita (about 1217 to 1255) is the founder of the Mali Empire, known largely from oral tradition, especially the Epic of Sundiata.

His story was preserved and performed by griots, hereditary oral historians.

Historians treat details of the epic with caution.

person/sunni-ali.title: Sunni Ali
person/sunni-ali.summary: Sunni Ali (ruled about 1464 to 1492) was the ruler who turned Songhai from a small state on the Niger River into a West African empire, taking Timbuktu in 1468 as the Mali Empire declined. His birth year is unknown.
facts: Sunni Ali became ruler of Songhai about 1464, the fifteenth in the Sunni dynasty.
He conquered Timbuktu in 1468 and, after a long siege, the trading city of Djenné, taking advantage of the weakening Mali Empire.
He was nominally Muslim but tolerated older local religious practice, and this drew tension with Muslim scholars in Timbuktu, whose chronicles remember him harshly.
He died in 1492; accounts differ on whether he drowned crossing a river or died another way.
His son Sunni Baru succeeded him but was overthrown in 1493 by Askia Muhammad, a general who accused Sunni Baru of insufficient devotion to Islam and founded a new dynasty.
person/sunni-ali.context: Sunni Ali built the Songhai Empire in Sub-Saharan Africa during the Medieval Period, seizing Timbuktu as the Mali Empire weakened. See War and Conflict and Religion and Belief.
person/sunni-ali.observer: The Observer notes that the harshest account of Sunni Ali comes from the Muslim scholars of the city he conquered, whose meaning-engine he did not fully adopt, so the record of his reign carries their grievance along with the facts. His death drew two different stories within a generation, a sign of how quickly detail slips even for a ruling conqueror. A specialist could argue that the Timbuktu chronicles' harsh portrait reflects the scholars' own resentment more than his actual governance, which would weaken a reading of him as simply irreligious.
questions: How did Sunni Ali die, and why do the accounts differ?
How much of his reputation for irreligion reflects the political grievance of Timbuktu's scholars rather than his actual practice?

[Wikipedia on Sonni Ali; Wikipedia on Songhai Empire]

2026-09-27: His death on 6 November 1492 is a matter of conjecture: the Tarikh al-Sudan says he drowned in a boating accident crossing the Niger, while oral tradition says his sister's son Askia Muhammad Ture killed him. [Wikipedia on Sonni Ali]

[Wikipedia on Sonni Ali]

person/tamar-of-georgia.title: Tamar of Georgia
person/tamar-of-georgia.summary: Tamar (born about 1160 or 1166, died 1213) ruled the Kingdom of Georgia from 1184 to 1213, presiding over its political and cultural high point, later called the Georgian Golden Age.
facts: She was crowned co-ruler with her father, George III, in 1178 to secure her succession, then became sole monarch on his death in 1184, ruling with the formal title "king of kings" rather than a feminine equivalent.

Her armies won major victories against regional Muslim powers, including the Battle of Shamkor in 1195 and the Battle of Basian (dated to 1202, 1203 or 1204 depending on the source), expanding Georgian influence across much of the South Caucasus and into parts of Armenia and Anatolia.

Her reign saw significant patronage of Georgian literature and architecture, including the era's most celebrated work, Shota Rustaveli's epic poem "The Knight in the Panther's Skin," traditionally associated with her as its inspiration.
She was canonized as a saint by the Georgian Orthodox Church, and centuries of later Georgian tradition remember her reign as the kingdom's greatest period of security and cultural achievement.
person/tamar-of-georgia.context: Tamar ruled Georgia in the Levant and Anatolia region during the Medieval Period, expanding Georgian power at the expense of neighboring Muslim states. See Religion and Belief, War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/tamar-of-georgia.observer: The Observer notes that Tamar's title, "king" rather than "queen," suggests Georgian tradition saw sovereignty itself as inherently masculine even while accepting a woman as its holder, a distinction that separates the office from the person occupying it more sharply than modern titles usually do.
questions: How much of Georgia's "Golden Age" reputation reflects Tamar's own governance versus favorable regional conditions, including the temporary weakness of neighboring powers?

person/teddy-roosevelt.title: Teddy Roosevelt
person/teddy-roosevelt.summary: Theodore "Teddy" Roosevelt (1858 to 1919) was the 26th President of the United States, serving from 1901 to 1909, known for trust-busting antitrust policy, an assertive foreign policy, and a major expansion of federal land conservation.
facts: He became president in 1901 after the assassination of William McKinley, at 42 the youngest person to hold the office, and was elected in his own right in 1904.

He pursued antitrust action against major corporate combinations, including a successful suit against the Northern Securities Company railroad trust in 1904, and mediated the 1902 coal strike partly by threatening to send in federal troops to run the mines.

He established the United States Forest Service and used his executive authority to create national forests, wildlife refuges, and national monuments, protecting roughly 230 million acres of land during his presidency.
After leaving office he attempted a comeback in the 1912 election on a progressive "Bull Moose" third-party ticket, splitting the Republican vote and helping elect Woodrow Wilson instead.
person/teddy-roosevelt.context: Theodore Roosevelt led the United States, in North America, during the Industrial Age. See Earth Systems and Life, War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/teddy-roosevelt.observer: The Observer notes that Roosevelt's conservation legacy, protecting land at a scale no predecessor had attempted, came from the same expansive view of executive power that also let him intervene directly in labor disputes and corporate affairs; the same instinct toward vigorous federal action that alarmed his political opponents also produced the national park and forest system many now take for granted.
questions: How much of Roosevelt's conservation program would have been achievable through Congress alone, without his willingness to act through executive authority?

person/timur.title: Timur
person/timur.summary: Timur (Tamerlane, traditionally dated 1336 to 1405) was a Central Asian conqueror who built the Timurid Empire and made Samarkand its centre.
facts: Timur's birth year is contested: 1336 is the traditional date, but many contemporary accounts imply the late 1320s. He was born near Kesh (now Shahrisabz, Uzbekistan).
By about 1370 he had besieged his rival Amir Husayn at Balkh and, after Husayn's assassination, proclaimed himself sovereign of the Chagatai line of khans, with dominion over Transoxiana.

He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan and did not take the title khan. He ruled as amir through a puppet Chaghatayid khan, Suyurghatmish, and took the title güregen (royal son-in-law) through his marriage to Saray Mulk Khanum, of the Chinggisid line.
His armies campaigned in Persia, Iraq, the lands of the Golden Horde, India (Delhi was sacked in 1398), and Anatolia (he defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at Ankara in 1402).
Later chronicles describe massacres in cities he conquered. Their casualty figures are contested (see Open Questions).

He died in February 1405 at Otrar (also called Farab), in present-day Kazakhstan, while preparing an invasion of Ming China. Sources differ on the day (17 to 19 February). He was buried in the Gur-e-Amir in Samarkand.
person/timur.context: Timur founded the Timurid Empire and presented himself as a restorer of the Mongol empire of Genghis Khan. He rebuilt Samarkand, where he deported artisans from conquered cities.
person/timur.observer: The Observer notes a conqueror who could not claim descent from the earlier conqueror he admired, and so bought the link instead: a Genghisid wife, a puppet khan, and the title of son-in-law. Legitimacy borrowed through marriage rather than blood is still a form of ancestor-weight, and it suggests the pull of the earlier line was strong enough to be worth acquiring.
questions: How reliable are the casualty figures in accounts of his campaigns? Chronicle figures for single cities run from tens of thousands to over a hundred thousand, and modern scholars estimate millions of deaths overall, but none of these numbers is well established.
When was he actually born: the late 1320s or 1336?

person/tokugawa-ieyasu.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu
person/tokugawa-ieyasu.summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543 to 1616) unified Japan after decades of civil war and founded the Tokugawa shogunate, a military government that ruled Japan for over two and a half centuries.
facts: He rose through alliance and conflict with the era's other major warlords, Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi, before defeating a rival coalition at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.
He was appointed shogun by the emperor in 1603, then formally passed the title to his son Hidetada in 1605 while continuing to hold real power as retired shogun until his death.
He destroyed the remaining Toyotomi family stronghold at the siege of Osaka Castle in 1615, removing the last major rival claim to national authority.

His government issued regulations restricting Christianity and foreign trade that his successors expanded into the sakoku ("closed country") policy, limiting most foreign contact for over two centuries.
person/tokugawa-ieyasu.context: Tokugawa Ieyasu founded the Tokugawa Shogunate in East Asia during the Early Modern Period, ending the Sengoku period of civil war. See War and Conflict, Trade and Economy and Kinship and Society.
person/tokugawa-ieyasu.observer: The Observer notes that Ieyasu's caution and willingness to wait out rivals rather than defeat them quickly are often credited for his success where more aggressive contemporaries failed; a well-known adage from the era compares Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and Ieyasu by how each supposedly answered a caged bird that would not sing, with Ieyasu simply waiting for it to sing on its own.
questions: How deliberate was the shift toward isolationism under his immediate successors, versus a gradual response to specific incidents involving European traders and missionaries?
fact_checks: 2026-09-27: Tokugawa Ieyasu was born on 31 January 1543 at Okazaki Castle and died on 1 June 1616 at Sunpu Castle, aged 73. [Wikipedia on Tokugawa Ieyasu]
2026-09-27: Ieyasu was appointed shogun on 24 March 1603 and resigned on 16 April 1605, but held de facto control of the government until his death in 1616. [Wikipedia on Tokugawa Ieyasu]

2026-09-27: The Battle of Sekigahara was fought on 21 October 1600 between Ieyasu's Eastern Army and the Western Army loyal to Ishida Mitsunari, ended in an Eastern Army victory, and is generally considered the beginning point of the Tokugawa shogunate; Emperor Go-Yozei made Ieyasu shogun in 1603. [Wikipedia on Battle of Sekigahara]

2026-09-27: The Siege of Osaka ran from a winter campaign (8 November 1614 to 22 January 1615) to a summer campaign (May to June 1615), when Toyotomi Hideyori and Yodo-dono died in the burning Osaka Castle, ending the Toyotomi dynasty and the last major armed opposition to the Tokugawa shogunate. [Wikipedia on Siege of Osaka]

2026-09-27: The Tokugawa shogunate governed Japan from 1603 to 1868 (265 years); Ieyasu banned Catholicism completely in 1614, and the sakoku seclusion laws came only after 1635, limiting inbound ships to those from China, Korea and the Netherlands. [Wikipedia on Tokugawa shogunate]

person/tomyris.title: Tomyris
person/tomyris.summary: Tomyris was a queen of the Massagetae, a nomadic people east of the Caspian Sea, who according to the Greek historian Herodotus defeated and killed Cyrus the Great of Persia in 530 BCE. She is known only from Herodotus, and other ancient accounts of Cyrus's death differ.
facts: Tomyris appears only in Book 1 of Herodotus's Histories, written about a century after the events. Her dates are unknown; the date given here is that of the battle in his account.
Herodotus says she ruled the Massagetae, who lived east of the Caspian Sea near the Araxes River, and rejected Cyrus's offer of marriage, which he saw as a way to gain her kingdom.
In his account the Persians captured her son Spargapises by trickery, and he killed himself in captivity. Tomyris then defeated the Persian army in battle.
Herodotus says she had Cyrus's body found and his head put in a wineskin filled with blood.
Other ancient accounts differ: Xenophon has Cyrus die peacefully in his palace, and Ctesias has him die of a wound in a war on the eastern frontier that the Persians won.
Herodotus compares the Massagetae's customs with those of the Scythians.
person/tomyris.context: Tomyris's story concerns the death of Cyrus the Great, founder of the Achaemenid Persians, on the Central Asian Steppe frontier during the Iron Age. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/tomyris.observer: The Observer notes that Tomyris survives only through an outsider's account that gives a steppe queen a speech and a grim revenge, a story-glue for Greek readers about the limits of a great king. That the tale turns on a mother's lost son shows how the kin-lattice gave it meaning. The reading would weaken if steppe or archaeological evidence showed a different ruler, or if the Persian defeat proved to be invented.
questions: What do archaeology and steppe sources add about the Massagetae?

person/toussaint-louverture.title: Toussaint Louverture
person/toussaint-louverture.summary: Toussaint Louverture was a formerly enslaved man who became the principal military and political leader of the Haitian Revolution, and died in a French prison in 1803.
facts: He was born into slavery on Saint-Domingue around 1743 (20 May 1743 in one account) and was freed in 1776 or 1777, depending on the source, before the revolution began in 1791.

He began as a lieutenant in the 1791 uprising and at first allied with the Spanish of neighboring Santo Domingo. In 1794 he switched to the French Republic, which had abolished slavery, and in 1798 he negotiated the withdrawal of British forces under a treaty with General Thomas Maitland.
On 7 July 1801 he promulgated a constitution asserting his authority over the whole island of Hispaniola, which made him governor-general for life.
Napoleon sent an expedition in 1802; Toussaint was arrested by deception and deported to France, where he died at Fort de Joux in April 1803.
Jean-Jacques Dessalines proclaimed Haiti's independence on 1 January 1804.
person/toussaint-louverture.context: Toussaint was the central figure of the Haitian Revolution, an event within the Age of Revolutions that led to Abolition of Slavery in Saint-Domingue. Toussaint Louverture sits in the Industrial Age and the region Caribbean and Atlantic World, and belongs to the theme thread of War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/toussaint-louverture.observer: The Observer notes that a man born into slavery wrote a constitution and commanded armies, and that the empire he fought treated his rights as negotiable by treachery. The universal principles proclaimed in that era were tested most severely by people who were excluded from them.
questions: How far did his constitution intend independence?

person/trajan.title: Trajan
person/trajan.summary: Trajan (53 to 117 CE) was Roman emperor from 98 to 117, presiding over the empire's greatest territorial extent and a major program of public building and infrastructure across the Roman world.
facts: Born in Hispania, in present-day Spain, he was the first Roman emperor born outside Italy, adopted as heir by the emperor Nerva in 97 after a career as a successful general.
His conquest of Dacia, commemorated in the reliefs of Trajan's Column in Rome, added a wealthy new province rich in gold mines north of the Danube.

He extended Roman territory to its largest extent by annexing Armenia and parts of Mesopotamia after a campaign against the Parthian Empire late in his reign, gains his successor Hadrian largely abandoned as unsustainable.
His building programs included Trajan's Forum and Market in Rome, a new harbor at Ostia, and an extensive network of roads and bridges across the provinces, funded substantially by Dacian gold.
person/trajan.context: Trajan led the Romans from the Mediterranean Basin during Classical Antiquity, expanding the empire to its widest extent. See War and Conflict, Technology and Trade and Economy.
person/trajan.observer: The Observer notes that Trajan's eastern conquests, which later Roman writers celebrated as the empire's high-water mark, were abandoned within a year of his death by his own successor as indefensible; the empire's territorial peak and its practical limits were reached almost simultaneously.
questions: Would Trajan's eastern conquests have proven sustainable had he lived longer to consolidate them, or was Hadrian's withdrawal the more realistic assessment?

person/truganini.title: Truganini
person/truganini.summary: Truganini (about 1812 to 1876) was a Tasmanian Aboriginal woman of the Nuenonne people who grew up on Bruny Island and lived through the British colonization of Tasmania and died in Hobart. She was later widely called "the last Tasmanian Aboriginal," a label that Tasmanian Aboriginal people reject.
facts: Truganini was born about 1812, reportedly at Recherche Bay in southern Tasmania, as a member of the Nuenonne people, and she grew up on Bruny Island.
Accounts say members of her family were killed or abducted by colonists during the Black War of the 1820s and early 1830s.
In the 1830s she worked with George Augustus Robinson, a government-appointed conciliator who persuaded surviving Aboriginal people to move to Flinders Island, where disease and hardship were severe.
She later lived at Oyster Cove, south of Hobart, and died on 8 May 1876.
Her skeleton was exhumed in 1878 and displayed in the Tasmanian Museum from 1904 until 1947, despite her reported fear of mutilation.
In 1976 her remains were cremated and the ashes scattered in the D'Entrecasteaux Channel.
Tasmanian Aboriginal people today descend from other women, such as Fanny Cochrane Smith, and the community continues.
person/truganini.context: Truganini's life falls within the British colonization that followed the First Fleet and the Colonization of Australia, which reshaped the lives of the Aboriginal Australians in Oceania during the Industrial Age. See War and Conflict and Kinship and Society.
person/truganini.observer: The Observer notes that Truganini's life is documented almost entirely by colonial officials, and that the record of her last decades is dominated by what was done to her body after death, when her own wishes about burial were not honored. The phrase "the last Tasmanian" turned a living community into an ending, a story-glue that served the settlers' account of what had happened. A specialist could argue that the label reflects a narrow test of descent, and that this reading understates how much of her own aim can be recovered.
questions: What can Aboriginal oral histories add to the colonial record of her life?
